Correct: 200 is also higher than 110, so this static route is installed only when OSPF no longer offers 10.50.0.0/24.
explanation: A floating static route must have the same prefix and length as the route it backs up and an administrative distance higher than that route's source (above 110 for OSPF).

question: Refer to the exhibit. R1 has two Internet links. The link to 203.0.113.1 must be the primary path and the link to 198.51.100.1 must be used only as a backup. Both links are up, but all Internet traffic leaves through 198.51.100.1. Which change corrects the problem?
exhibit:
R1# show running-config | include ip route
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.1 10
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 198.51.100.1 5
R1# show ip route static
<output omitted>
Gateway of last resort is 198.51.100.1 to network 0.0.0.0

S*    0.0.0.0/0 [5/0] via 198.51.100.1
options: Swap the order of the two commands in the configuration so that the backup route is listed first.
Reconfigure the route through 203.0.113.1 with an administrative distance of 255.
Remove the administrative distance from both routes so that the first one configured is preferred.
Reconfigure the route through 198.51.100.1 with an administrative distance higher than 10, such as 20.
rationales: Wrong: the order of the commands has no effect. For the same prefix IOS installs the static route with the lowest administrative distance.
Wrong: a route with an administrative distance of 255 is never installed in the routing table, so the primary path would never be used.
Wrong: with equal distances both default routes are installed and R1 load-shares over both links, which is not a primary and backup design.
Correct: the backup route has distance 5 and the primary has 10, so the backup is winning. Giving the backup a higher value than the primary makes it float until the primary is removed.
explanation: Between two static routes to the same prefix, the lower administrative distance is installed. The backup (floating) route must always carry the higher value.

question: Refer to the exhibit. The remote site behind 10.0.12.2 uses the address block 10.30.4.0/22. From R1, hosts in part of the block are unreachable. Which command should replace the existing static route?
exhibit:
R1# show ip route static
<output omitted>
Gateway of last resort is not set

      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 3 subnets, 3 masks
S        10.30.4.0/24 [1/0] via 10.0.12.2
R1# ping 10.30.4.10
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 5, 100-byte ICMP Echos to 10.30.4.10, timeout is 2 seconds:
!!!!!
Success rate is 100 percent (5/5), round-trip min/avg/max = 1/1/2 ms
R1# ping 10.30.6.10
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 5, 100-byte ICMP Echos to 10.30.6.10, timeout is 2 seconds:
.....
Success rate is 0 percent (0/5)
rationales: Correct: a /22 is 255.255.252.0, which covers 10.30.4.0 to 10.30.7.255 and therefore includes 10.30.6.10.
Wrong: 255.255.254.0 is a /23, covering only 10.30.4.0 to 10.30.5.255, so 10.30.6.10 would still have no route.
Wrong: 255.255.248.0 is a /21, and 10.30.4.0 is not a /21 network boundary, so IOS rejects the command as an inconsistent address and mask.
Wrong: 0.0.3.255 is the wildcard form of a /22. The ip route command requires a subnet mask, so this is rejected.
explanation: The configured mask of 255.255.255.0 covers only 10.30.4.0/24, so the rest of the /22 has no route. A static route's mask must match the real size of the remote block: /22 is 255.255.252.0.

question: Refer to the exhibit. R1 (10.0.12.1) and R2 (10.0.12.2) are directly connected. Hosts on the R1 LAN 192.168.10.0/24 cannot reach the server 192.168.20.10 on the R2 LAN. Which command resolves the problem?
exhibit:
R1# ping 192.168.20.10
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 5, 100-byte ICMP Echos to 192.168.20.10, timeout is 2 seconds:
!!!!!
Success rate is 100 percent (5/5), round-trip min/avg/max = 1/1/1 ms
R1# ping 192.168.20.10 source GigabitEthernet0/1
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 5, 100-byte ICMP Echos to 192.168.20.10, timeout is 2 seconds:
Packet sent with a source address of 192.168.10.1
.....
Success rate is 0 percent (0/5)

R2# show ip route
<output omitted>
Gateway of last resort is not set

      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 2 subnets, 2 masks
C        10.0.12.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        10.0.12.2/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
      192.168.20.0/24 is variably subnetted, 2 subnets, 2 masks
C        192.168.20.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
L        192.168.20.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
rationales: Correct: R2 has no route to 192.168.10.0/24 and no default route, so replies to sources in that LAN are dropped. A static route back through R1 at 10.0.12.1 completes the return path.
Wrong: 10.0.12.2 is R2's own interface address. The next hop must be the address of the neighbouring router, 10.0.12.1.
Wrong: 192.168.20.0/24 is directly connected to R2. Pointing it at R1 does nothing for the missing route to 192.168.10.0/24.
Wrong: the first ping succeeds, which proves R1 already has a working route to 192.168.20.0/24. The forward path is not the fault.
explanation: A ping that works from the link address but fails when sourced from the LAN shows one-way routing: the far router can reach the link subnet but has no return route to the LAN. Static routes are needed in both directions.

question: An engineer sees an IPv4 static route in the running configuration of R1, but the route is missing from the output of show ip route. Which two conditions cause this? (Choose two.)
options: R1 has no route in its routing table that covers the configured next-hop address.
A routing protocol offers the same prefix with a higher administrative distance than the static route.
The LAN interface for the destination network is shut down on the remote router.
The exit interface named in the static route is down.
The next-hop router has no route back to the networks behind R1.
rationales: Correct: a static route with a next-hop address is installed only if R1 can resolve that address through another route, normally a connected one. An unresolvable next hop keeps the route out of the table.
Wrong: the lower administrative distance wins, so the static route would be installed and the routing protocol's route would be the one left out.
Wrong: a static route carries no information about the far end. R1 keeps the route installed even when the remote network itself is down.
Correct: a static route that points to an exit interface is installed only while that interface is up. When the interface goes down the route is withdrawn from the table.
Wrong: a missing return route causes one-way traffic, but R1 cannot see the neighbour's table and still installs its own static route.
explanation: IOS installs a static route only when it is usable locally: the exit interface must be up and any next-hop address must be resolvable in the routing table. Nothing beyond the local router is checked.

question: Refer to the exhibit. How does R1 forward a packet destined for 10.2.7.7?
exhibit:
R1# show ip route
<output omitted>
Gateway of last resort is not set

      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 6 subnets, 4 masks
C        10.0.12.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        10.0.12.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
C        10.0.13.0/30 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
L        10.0.13.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/1
S        10.2.0.0/16 [1/0] via 10.9.9.9
O        10.9.9.0/24 [110/2] via 10.0.13.2, 00:15:36, GigabitEthernet0/1
options: It looks up 10.9.9.9, finds the OSPF route to 10.9.9.0/24, and sends the packet out of GigabitEthernet0/1 to 10.0.13.2.
It sends the packet out of GigabitEthernet0/0 to 10.0.12.2, because that is the lowest-numbered interface.
It sends ARP requests for 10.9.9.9 out of both GigabitEthernet interfaces and uses the one that answers.
It drops the packet, because the next hop 10.9.9.9 is not in a directly connected subnet.
rationales: Correct: the static route gives only a next-hop address, so R1 performs a recursive lookup. 10.9.9.9 matches 10.9.9.0/24, which supplies the real next hop 10.0.13.2 and the outgoing interface.
Wrong: interface numbering plays no part. The outgoing interface comes from the route that resolves the next hop.
Wrong: a router sends ARP only for addresses in a connected subnet. 10.9.9.9 is reached through the OSPF route, so R1 uses ARP for 10.0.13.2 instead.
Wrong: a static next hop does not have to be directly connected. The route is installed, as the exhibit shows, because 10.9.9.9 can be resolved through another route.
explanation: A static route that names only a next hop is recursive: the router looks the next hop up again until it reaches a route with an outgoing interface. If that resolving route is lost, the static route is removed as well.

question: R1 has a primary static route with the default administrative distance and a floating static route to the same prefix with an administrative distance of 200. Put the events in the order they occur when the primary link fails and later recovers.
items: Only the primary static route is in the routing table; the floating route exists only in the configuration.
The interface used to reach the primary next hop goes down.
R1 removes the primary static route because its next hop can no longer be resolved.
R1 installs the floating static route, shown with [200/0], and traffic moves to the backup path.
The interface comes back up and the primary static route is reinstalled, displacing the floating route.
explanation: While the primary route (AD 1) is usable, the floating route (AD 200) stays out of the table. When the primary interface fails, the primary route is withdrawn and the floating route takes over. When the interface recovers, the route with the lower administrative distance returns and the floating route is removed from the table again.

question: R1 has IPv6 addresses on two LAN interfaces, both up, and correct IPv6 static routes. Hosts on each LAN can ping the R1 interface on their own LAN, but R1 does not forward IPv6 packets between the LANs. IPv4 traffic is routed normally. Which command is missing from R1?
options: ipv6 enable
ipv6 address autoconfig
ipv6 unicast-routing
ip routing
rationales: Wrong: ipv6 enable is an interface command that only creates a link-local address. The interfaces already have IPv6 addresses and are answering pings.
Wrong: ipv6 address autoconfig makes an interface obtain its own address by SLAAC. It does not make the router forward packets.
Correct: this global command turns on IPv6 packet forwarding. Without it the router answers for its own IPv6 addresses, like a host, but does not route IPv6 between interfaces.
Wrong: ip routing controls IPv4 forwarding, which is on by default on a router and is already working here.
explanation: IPv4 routing is enabled by default on a router, but IPv6 forwarding is not: ipv6 unicast-routing must be configured globally before the router forwards IPv6 packets or runs an IPv6 routing protocol.

question: Refer to the exhibit. The neighbour with the link-local address FE80::2 is reached through GigabitEthernet0/0. Which command does R1 accept for this static route?
exhibit:
R1(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:50::/64 fe80::2
% Interface has to be specified for a link-local nexthop
options: ipv6 route 2001:db8:50::/64 GigabitEthernet0/0 fe80::2
ipv6 route 2001:db8:50::/64 fe80::2 GigabitEthernet0/0
ipv6 route 2001:db8:50::/64 fe80::2 link-local
rationales: Correct: a link-local next hop must be given as a fully specified route, with the exit interface first and the next-hop address after it.
Wrong: a next hop is a single address and takes no prefix length, and this still gives R1 no interface to use.
Wrong: the elements are in the wrong order. In a fully specified route the interface comes before the next-hop address.
Wrong: there is no link-local keyword in the ipv6 route command. The interface is what tells R1 which link FE80::2 is on.
explanation: Every interface is in FE80::/10, so a link-local address alone does not identify a link. A static route to a link-local next hop must be fully specified: ipv6 route prefix/length interface next-hop.

question: Which command configures an IPv6 default static route that uses the next hop 2001:db8:0:12::2?
rationales: Correct: ::/0 is the all-zeros prefix with a length of 0, which matches every IPv6 destination.
Wrong: 2001:db8::/32 matches only addresses that begin with 2001:db8, so every other destination would still have no route.
Wrong: ::/128 is a host route to the single unspecified address ::, not a route for all destinations.
Wrong: ip route configures IPv4 static routes only. IPv6 static routes use the ipv6 route command.
explanation: The IPv6 default route is ::/0, the equivalent of 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 in IPv4. IPv6 static routes use ipv6 route with prefix-length notation.

question: Traffic for one dual-stack server, 10.40.1.25 and 2001:db8:40::25, must be sent to the next hops 10.0.14.2 and 2001:db8:0:14::2. All other hosts in the server's subnets must keep using the existing network routes. Which two commands meet the requirement? (Choose two.)
rationales: Correct: a mask of 255.255.255.255 (/32) creates an IPv4 host route that matches only 10.40.1.25. As the longest match it overrides the network route for that one address.
Wrong: a /64 prefix length describes the whole subnet 2001:db8:40::/64, not a single host, so this is not a host route.
Correct: a prefix length of /128 creates an IPv6 host route that matches only 2001:db8:40::25.
Wrong: 0.0.0.0 is not a host mask. It looks like the wildcard for a single host in an ACL, but static routes use subnet masks, and IOS rejects this address and mask combination.
Wrong: this is a network route for the whole of 10.40.1.0/24, so it would affect every host in the subnet rather than just the server.
explanation: A host route matches exactly one address: mask 255.255.255.255 for IPv4 and prefix length /128 for IPv6. Being the longest possible match, it always beats a network route for that address.

question: Refer to the exhibit. R1 connects to R2 over 10.0.12.0/30 (R1 is .1, R2 is .2) and to R3 over 10.0.13.0/30 (R1 is .1, R3 is .2). The LAN 192.168.30.0/24 is attached to R3 only. Which two commands on R1 are needed to restore reachability to that LAN? (Choose two.)
exhibit:
R1# show ip route static
<output omitted>
Gateway of last resort is not set

S     192.168.30.0/24 [1/0] via 10.0.12.2
R1# traceroute 192.168.30.10
Type escape sequence to abort.
Tracing the route to 192.168.30.10
VRF info: (vrf in name/id, vrf out name/id)
  1 10.0.12.2 1 msec 1 msec 0 msec
  2 10.0.12.2 !H  *  !H
rationales: Correct: the existing route sends the traffic to R2, which has no route to the LAN and answers with host unreachable (!H). If it were left in place beside the new route, R1 would load-share and still lose the packets sent to R2.
Wrong: 10.0.13.1 is R1's own address on the link to R3. A next hop must be the neighbour's address, not a local one.
Wrong: this still points at R2, the wrong router. Changing the administrative distance does not change where the packets are sent.
Correct: the LAN is behind R3, so the next hop must be R3's address on the shared link, 10.0.13.2.
Wrong: a default route to R2 also points at the wrong router, and the more specific /24 static route would still be used for this LAN anyway.
explanation: The traceroute stops at 10.0.12.2 with !H, so R1 is handing the packets to a router that has no route for them: the static route has the wrong next hop. Remove the faulty route as well as adding the correct one, or both stay installed with the same administrative distance.

question: Refer to the exhibit. R1 connects to R2 on GigabitEthernet0/0 and to R3 on GigabitEthernet0/1. The network 2001:db8:50::/64 is attached to R3, and ipv6 unicast-routing is enabled on all routers. What is the cause of the failed ping?
exhibit:
R1# show running-config | include ipv6 route
ipv6 route 2001:DB8:50::/64 GigabitEthernet0/0 FE80::3
R1# show ipv6 route static
<output omitted>
S   2001:DB8:50::/64 [1/0]
     via FE80::3, GigabitEthernet0/0
R1# show ipv6 neighbors
IPv6 Address                              Age Link-layer Addr State Interface
FE80::2                                     0 5254.00a1.0002  REACH Gi0/0
FE80::3                                     0 5254.00a1.0003  REACH Gi0/1
FE80::3                                     0 -               INCMP Gi0/0
R1# ping 2001:db8:50::10
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 5, 100-byte ICMP Echos to 2001:DB8:50::10, timeout is 2 seconds:
.....
Success rate is 0 percent (0/5)
options: A link-local address cannot be used as the next hop of a static route; a global unicast next hop is required.
The static route names the wrong exit interface; FE80::3 is reachable through GigabitEthernet0/1, not GigabitEthernet0/0.
The static route has not been installed in the routing table, because GigabitEthernet0/0 is down.
The exit interface and the next-hop address are entered in the wrong order in the ipv6 route command.
rationales: Wrong: link-local next hops are valid for IPv6 static routes, provided the correct exit interface is given with them.

Correct: the neighbour table shows FE80::3 reachable on Gi0/1 but incomplete (INCMP) on Gi0/0. The route tells R1 to look for FE80::3 on the R2 link, where no device owns that address, so the packets cannot be delivered.
Wrong: the route is present in show ipv6 route static, and the neighbour FE80::2 is reachable on Gi0/0, so that interface is up.
Wrong: the order is correct. A fully specified IPv6 static route lists the interface first and then the next-hop address.
explanation: A link-local next hop is only meaningful on the link named in the route. If the exit interface is wrong, the route is still installed while that interface is up, but neighbour discovery for the next hop fails and traffic is lost. Correct it with ipv6 route 2001:db8:50::/64 GigabitEthernet0/1 fe80::3.

question: Refer to the exhibit. R1 connects to its provider's router, 203.0.113.1, over an Ethernet link on GigabitEthernet1. Internet access stopped working after the provider disabled proxy ARP on its router. Which change on R1 restores connectivity?
exhibit:
R1# show running-config | include ip route
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 GigabitEthernet1
R1# show ip route static
<output omitted>
Gateway of last resort is 0.0.0.0 to network 0.0.0.0

S*    0.0.0.0/0 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet1
R1# show ip arp
Protocol  Address          Age (min)  Hardware Addr   Type   Interface
Internet  192.0.2.80              0   Incomplete      ARPA
Internet  198.51.100.7            0   Incomplete      ARPA
Internet  203.0.113.1            12   5254.00b2.0001  ARPA   GigabitEthernet1
Internet  203.0.113.2             -   5254.00b2.0002  ARPA   GigabitEthernet1
options: Add the ip proxy-arp command to GigabitEthernet1 on R1.
Reconfigure the existing route with an administrative distance of 200.
Add the global command ip default-gateway 203.0.113.1.
Replace the route with ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 GigabitEthernet1 203.0.113.1.
rationales: Wrong: proxy ARP on R1 would let R1 answer ARP requests from other devices. It does not help R1 obtain answers to its own ARP requests for remote destinations.
Wrong: the route is already installed and selected. Changing its administrative distance does not change how R1 resolves the Layer 2 address for each destination.
Wrong: ip default-gateway is used only when IP routing is disabled. R1 is routing, so the command has no effect on forwarding.

Correct: with only an Ethernet exit interface, R1 treats every destination as directly connected and sends ARP for the destination itself, which works only if the neighbour answers with proxy ARP. Adding the next hop makes R1 resolve 203.0.113.1 instead, which is already in its ARP table.
explanation: On a multi-access (Ethernet) link, a static route that names only the exit interface makes the router ARP for every destination address and depend on proxy ARP. Give the next-hop address, alone or after the interface, so that only the neighbour's address has to be resolved.

question: R1 has three interfaces: G0/0 is 10.20.8.1/24, G0/1 is 10.20.11.1/24 and G0/2 is 10.20.12.1/24. An engineer must enable OSPF process 1 in area 0 on G0/0 and G0/1, but not on G0/2, using a single network statement. Which statement meets the requirement?
rationales: Wrong: 0.0.0.255 matches only 10.20.8.0 to 10.20.8.255, so G0/0 is enabled but G0/1 (10.20.11.1) is not.
Wrong: 0.0.7.255 is the inverse of /21 and matches 10.20.8.0 to 10.20.15.255, so G0/2 (10.20.12.1) would also run OSPF.
Correct: wildcard 0.0.3.255 is the inverse of 255.255.252.0 (/22), so it matches 10.20.8.0 to 10.20.11.255. That includes 10.20.8.1 and 10.20.11.1 but not 10.20.12.1.
Wrong: 0.0.15.255 is the inverse of /20 and matches 10.20.0.0 to 10.20.15.255, which includes all three interfaces.
explanation: The OSPF network command enables OSPF on every interface whose IP address falls inside the address/wildcard range. Wildcard = 255.255.255.255 minus the subnet mask, so a /22 block is 0.0.3.255.

question: R1 is reloaded with the configuration shown. Which router ID does OSPF process 1 use?
exhibit:
R1# show running-config
<output omitted>
interface Loopback0
 ip address 10.255.0.1 255.255.255.255
!
interface Loopback1
 ip address 172.16.1.1 255.255.255.255
!
interface Loopback2
 ip address 198.51.100.1 255.255.255.255
 shutdown
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 203.0.113.9 255.255.255.252
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 192.168.50.1 255.255.255.0
!
router ospf 1
 network 192.168.50.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
 network 203.0.113.8 0.0.0.3 area 0
rationales: Correct: there is no router-id command, so OSPF takes the highest IP address on a loopback that is up. Loopback2 is shut down, which leaves 172.16.1.1 as the highest.
Wrong: 203.0.113.9 is the highest address on an active physical interface, but physical interfaces are only considered when no loopback is up.
Wrong: 198.51.100.1 is the highest loopback address, but Loopback2 is administratively down and a down interface cannot supply the router ID.
Wrong: the loopback number is irrelevant. OSPF compares the IP addresses, and 10.255.0.1 is lower than 172.16.1.1.
explanation: Router ID order: 1) the router-id command, 2) the highest IP address on an up loopback, 3) the highest IP address on an up physical interface. The interface does not need to be advertised in OSPF.

question: R1 runs OSPF process 1 with router ID 192.168.1.1 and has full adjacencies. An engineer enters 'router-id 10.0.0.1' under 'router ospf 1', but 'show ip protocols' still shows router ID 192.168.1.1. Which two actions would each make R1 start using 10.0.0.1? (Choose two.)
options: Enter 'clear ip route *' in privileged EXEC mode
Wait for the 40-second dead interval to expire
Save the configuration and reload the router
Enter 'clear ip ospf process' in privileged EXEC mode and confirm
Enter 'shutdown' and then 'no shutdown' on the interface that owns 192.168.1.1
rationales: Wrong: this only clears and rebuilds the IP routing table. The OSPF process and its router ID are untouched.
Wrong: the dead interval only decides when a silent neighbour is declared down. It has no effect on router ID selection.
Correct: after a reload the OSPF process starts fresh and reads the saved router-id command.
Correct: restarting the OSPF process makes it select its router ID again, and the configured router-id command now takes priority.
Wrong: a running OSPF process keeps its router ID even when the interface it was taken from flaps, and it does not re-read the router-id command when an interface bounces.
explanation: The router ID is chosen when the OSPF process starts and then stays fixed. IOS tells you to reload or use 'clear ip ospf process' for a new router-id to take effect. Clearing the process drops the adjacencies briefly.

question: R1 and R2 are connected by an Ethernet link and both run OSPFv2. Which two differences between the routers would prevent them from becoming neighbours? (Choose two.)
options: R1 has OSPF priority 1 on the link and R2 has OSPF priority 0
R1 uses 'router ospf 1' and R2 uses 'router ospf 2'
R1 places the link in area 0 and R2 places it in area 1
R1 sends hellos every 10 seconds and R2 sends hellos every 5 seconds
R1 has OSPF cost 1 on the link and R2 has OSPF cost 10
rationales: Wrong: priority only affects the DR/BDR election. R2 simply cannot become DR or BDR, and the two routers still reach the FULL state.
Wrong: the process ID is only locally significant. It is not sent in OSPF packets and does not need to match.
Correct: the area ID is in the OSPF header and must be the same on both ends of a link.
Correct: hello and dead intervals are carried in every hello and must match, or the hello is ignored.
Wrong: cost is a local metric used in the SPF calculation. Different costs at each end are allowed and do not affect the adjacency.
explanation: To become OSPF neighbours two routers need the same area, the same subnet and mask, matching hello and dead timers and unique router IDs (and matching MTU to get past ExStart). Process ID, priority and cost do not have to match.

question: R1 and R2 do not list each other in 'show ip ospf neighbor'. The only OSPF timer command on either router is 'ip ospf hello-interval 5' on R2 G0/0. Which single change allows the adjacency to form?
exhibit:
R1# show ip ospf interface GigabitEthernet0/0
GigabitEthernet0/0 is up, line protocol is up
  Internet Address 10.1.12.1/30, Area 0, Attached via Network Statement
  Process ID 1, Router ID 1.1.1.1, Network Type BROADCAST, Cost: 1
  Transmit Delay is 1 sec, State DR, Priority 1
  Designated Router (ID) 1.1.1.1, Interface address 10.1.12.1
  No backup designated router on this network
  Timer intervals configured, Hello 10, Dead 40, Wait 40, Retransmit 5
<output omitted>

R2# show ip ospf interface GigabitEthernet0/0
GigabitEthernet0/0 is up, line protocol is up
  Internet Address 10.1.12.2/30, Area 0, Attached via Network Statement
  Process ID 1, Router ID 2.2.2.2, Network Type BROADCAST, Cost: 1
  Transmit Delay is 1 sec, State DR, Priority 1
  Designated Router (ID) 2.2.2.2, Interface address 10.1.12.2
  No backup designated router on this network
  Timer intervals configured, Hello 5, Dead 20, Wait 20, Retransmit 5
<output omitted>
options: On R2 G0/0: ip ospf dead-interval 40
On R1 G0/0: ip ospf dead-interval 20
On R2 G0/0: ip ospf hello-interval 10
On both G0/0 interfaces: ip ospf network point-to-point
rationales: Wrong: the dead intervals would both be 40 seconds, but R2 would still send hellos every 5 seconds while R1 expects 10.
Wrong: the dead intervals would both be 20 seconds, but the hello intervals would still be 10 and 5 seconds, and both timers must match.
Correct: R2 returns to a 10-second hello, and because no dead interval is set explicitly the dead interval follows at four times the hello (40 seconds). Both timers then match R1.
Wrong: this removes the DR election but does not touch the configured timers, so R2 would still use a 5-second hello against R1's 10 seconds.
explanation: Both the hello and the dead interval must match for OSPF neighbours to form. On IOS the dead interval defaults to four times the hello interval, so changing only the hello also moves the dead interval. Both routers claiming to be DR with no BDR is a sign that they are ignoring each other's hellos.

question: The adjacency between R1 and R2 never reaches FULL. What is the cause?
exhibit:
R1# show ip ospf neighbor

Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
2.2.2.2           1   EXSTART/DR      00:00:38    10.1.12.2       Ethernet0/1

R1# show ip interface Ethernet0/1 | include MTU
  MTU is 1500 bytes

R2# show ip interface Ethernet0/1 | include MTU
  MTU is 1400 bytes
options: The hello and dead timers differ on the two interfaces
R2 has OSPF priority 0 on the link, so it cannot exchange its database
The IP MTU differs on the two interfaces, so the database description packets are not accepted
The two interfaces are configured in different OSPF areas
rationales: Wrong: with mismatched timers the hellos are ignored, so the routers would never get as far as ExStart and R2 would not be listed at all.
Wrong: the Pri column shows 1, and R2 has even been elected DR. Priority 0 only stops a router from becoming DR or BDR.
Correct: the interface MTU is carried in DBD packets. With 1500 against 1400 the exchange cannot proceed and the neighbours stay in ExStart (or Exchange).
Wrong: hellos with a different area ID are discarded, so R2 would not appear in the neighbour table at all.
explanation: A neighbour stuck in EXSTART or EXCHANGE almost always means an MTU mismatch. Fix it by making the MTU the same on both ends (or, as a workaround, 'ip ospf mtu-ignore').

question: Put the OSPF neighbour states in the order two routers on an Ethernet segment pass through them while building a full adjacency, starting with the first.
explanation: Down (no hello heard), Init (hello heard), 2-Way (own router ID seen in the neighbour's hello), ExStart (master/slave decided), Exchange (DBD packets swapped), Loading (LSRs and LSUs fill the gaps), Full (databases synchronised).

question: Match each OSPF neighbour state to what is happening in that state.
pairs: A hello has arrived from the neighbour, but it does not yet list this router's ID
Each router has seen its own router ID in the other's hello; the DR and BDR are elected
The routers decide which one leads the database exchange and agree a starting sequence number
Database description (DBD) packets that summarise each LSDB are swapped
Link-state requests are sent for LSAs that are missing or out of date
The link-state databases of the two routers are synchronised
distractors: No hello has been heard from the neighbour within the dead interval
explanation: Init means one-way hellos. 2-Way means two-way hellos, and it is where the DR/BDR election takes place. ExStart sets master/slave and the first DBD sequence number, Exchange swaps DBD summaries, Loading uses LSR/LSU to fetch missing LSAs, and Full means the LSDBs match. Hearing no hello within the dead interval is the Down state.

question: R4 has router ID 10.0.0.4 and shares an Ethernet segment with three other OSPF routers. Which two conclusions does the output support? (Choose two.)
exhibit:
R4# show ip ospf neighbor

Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
10.0.0.5          1   2WAY/DROTHER    00:00:31    192.168.10.5    Ethernet0/0
10.0.0.6          1   FULL/BDR        00:00:33    192.168.10.6    Ethernet0/0
10.0.0.7          1   FULL/DR         00:00:37    192.168.10.7    Ethernet0/0
options: R4 and 10.0.0.5 have an MTU mismatch
R4 is a DROTHER on this segment
The 2WAY state with 10.0.0.5 is normal and needs no corrective action
R4 is not receiving hellos from 10.0.0.5
The router with ID 10.0.0.6 is currently the designated router
rationales: Wrong: an MTU mismatch shows up as a neighbour stuck in EXSTART or EXCHANGE, not as a stable 2WAY/DROTHER entry.
Correct: the DR (10.0.0.7) and the BDR (10.0.0.6) are both other routers, so R4 holds neither role and is a DROTHER.
Correct: two DROTHERs stay in 2-Way with each other. They only form full adjacencies with the DR and the BDR.
Wrong: 2-Way means hellos are flowing in both directions. If R4 heard nothing, 10.0.0.5 would not be listed.
Wrong: the role after the slash is the neighbour's role. 10.0.0.6 is the BDR, and 10.0.0.7 is the DR.
explanation: In 'show ip ospf neighbor' the State column shows the adjacency state and then the neighbour's role. On a broadcast segment a DROTHER is FULL with the DR and BDR and 2WAY with every other DROTHER, which is healthy.

question: Four OSPF routers on the same Ethernet LAN are powered on at the same time. R1 has priority 1 and router ID 10.0.0.1. R2 has priority 100 and router ID 10.0.0.2. R3 has priority 100 and router ID 10.0.0.3. R4 has priority 0 and router ID 10.0.0.4. Which routers become the DR and the BDR?
options: R3 is the DR and R4 is the BDR
R2 is the DR and R3 is the BDR
R4 is the DR and R3 is the BDR
R3 is the DR and R2 is the BDR
rationales: Wrong: R3 is the DR, but R4 has priority 0 and is not eligible to be the BDR.
Wrong: when priorities tie, the higher router ID wins, not the lower one.
Wrong: this picks the highest router IDs and ignores priority. R4 has priority 0, so it can never be DR or BDR.
Correct: the highest priority wins (R2 and R3 tie on 100) and the higher router ID breaks the tie, so R3 is the DR and R2 is the BDR.
explanation: DR/BDR election: highest interface priority first (default 1, range 0 to 255), then highest router ID. Priority 0 means the router never takes part in the election.

question: An engineer wants R3 to be the DR on its LAN and configures 'ip ospf priority 255' on Ethernet0/0. The output is taken five minutes later. Why is R3 still not the DR?
exhibit:
R3# show ip ospf interface Ethernet0/0
Ethernet0/0 is up, line protocol is up
  Internet Address 192.168.10.3/24, Area 0, Attached via Network Statement
  Process ID 1, Router ID 10.0.0.3, Network Type BROADCAST, Cost: 10
  Transmit Delay is 1 sec, State DROTHER, Priority 255
  Designated Router (ID) 10.0.0.1, Interface address 192.168.10.1
  Backup Designated router (ID) 10.0.0.2, Interface address 192.168.10.2
<output omitted>
options: A lower priority value is preferred, so 255 makes R3 the least likely DR
Priority 255 is reserved, so R3 is excluded from the election
The new priority is not active until 'clear ip ospf process' is entered on R3
The DR election is not preemptive, so the existing DR and BDR keep their roles until they fail or their OSPF processes restart
rationales: Wrong: the highest priority is preferred in the OSPF DR election.
Wrong: 255 is a valid priority and is the highest value. Only priority 0 excludes a router from the election.
Wrong: the output already shows Priority 255, so the value is active. Restarting OSPF on R3 alone changes nothing, because 10.0.0.1 and 10.0.0.2 would still hold the DR and BDR roles.
Correct: once a DR and BDR exist, a router with a better priority does not displace them. A new election only happens when the DR or BDR is lost.
explanation: OSPF DR/BDR roles are sticky. Priority only matters when an election actually runs. To move the DR role you must restart OSPF (or the interfaces) on the current DR and BDR; if only the DR fails, the BDR is promoted and the best remaining router becomes the new BDR.

question: Two routers are connected back to back on GigabitEthernet interfaces. The engineer wants OSPF to form the adjacency without holding a DR/BDR election on this link. Which interface command should be configured on both routers?
options: ip ospf network broadcast
ip ospf priority 0
ip ospf network point-to-point
ip ospf network non-broadcast
rationales: Wrong: broadcast is already the default on Ethernet, and it is the type that runs the DR/BDR election.
Wrong: with priority 0 on both routers nobody can become DR, but the network type is still broadcast, so the routers sit in 2-Way and never become fully adjacent.
Correct: the point-to-point network type has no DR or BDR, and the two routers go straight to a full adjacency.
Wrong: the non-broadcast type still elects a DR and BDR, and it also needs neighbours to be configured manually.
explanation: Ethernet interfaces default to the OSPF broadcast network type, which elects a DR and BDR. On a link with only two routers, 'ip ospf network point-to-point' removes the election; the neighbour then shows as FULL/ - .

question: R1, R2 and R3 all have 'auto-cost reference-bandwidth 10000' under their OSPF process. R1 reaches R2 through G0/0 (1 Gbps). R2 reaches R3 through Te0/1 (10 Gbps). R3's LAN interface G0/2 (1 Gbps) is in 10.9.9.0/24 and has 'ip ospf cost 50' configured. No other costs are changed. Which OSPF metric does R1 show for 10.9.9.0/24?
rationales: Wrong: 52 uses the default 100 Mbps reference bandwidth, which would make the 1 Gbps and 10 Gbps links cost 1 each. The reference bandwidth here is 10000 Mbps.
Correct: 10000/1000 = 10 for R1 G0/0, 10000/10000 = 1 for R2 Te0/1, and the manual cost of 50 on R3 G0/2. 10 + 1 + 50 = 61.
Wrong: 21 uses the calculated cost of 10 for R3 G0/2. The 'ip ospf cost 50' command overrides the calculated value on that interface.
Wrong: 11 adds only the two transit links and leaves out the cost of R3's interface on the destination network.
explanation: OSPF cost = reference bandwidth / interface bandwidth (default reference 100 Mbps, minimum cost 1), unless 'ip ospf cost' sets it by hand. The route metric is the sum of the outgoing interface costs along the path, including the interface on the destination network.

question: R2 G0/0 (10.1.12.2/30) connects to R1, and R2 G0/1 (192.168.20.1/24) connects to a user LAN. R1 is configured correctly, but R2 has no OSPF neighbour. Which change on R2 fixes the problem and still keeps OSPF hellos off the user LAN?
exhibit:
R2# show ip protocols
*** IP Routing is NSF aware ***

Routing Protocol is "ospf 1"
  Outgoing update filter list for all interfaces is not set
  Incoming update filter list for all interfaces is not set
  Router ID 2.2.2.2
  Number of areas in this router is 1. 1 normal 0 stub 0 nssa
  Maximum path: 4
  Routing for Networks:
    10.1.12.0 0.0.0.3 area 0
    192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
  Passive Interface(s):
    GigabitEthernet0/0
  Routing Information Sources:
    Gateway         Distance      Last Update
  Distance: (default is 110)
options: Under interface GigabitEthernet0/0: ip ospf priority 255
Under router ospf 1: network 10.1.12.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
Under router ospf 1: no passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/0, then passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/1
Under router ospf 1: passive-interface default
rationales: Wrong: priority only influences the DR/BDR election. A passive interface sends no hellos, whatever its priority.
Wrong: 10.1.12.2 is already matched by the existing network statement. The interface is in OSPF, but it is passive, so it sends no hellos.
Correct: the wrong interface was made passive. Removing it from G0/0 lets R2 send hellos to R1, and making G0/1 passive stops hellos on the user LAN while its subnet is still advertised.
Wrong: this makes every interface passive, including G0/0, so R2 would still have no neighbour.
explanation: A passive OSPF interface still has its subnet advertised, but it sends and processes no hellos, so no adjacency can form on it. Use it on LANs with no other OSPF routers, never on a link to a neighbour. 'show ip protocols' lists passive interfaces.

question: R1 has the static route 'ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.1' towards its ISP. Which command, entered under 'router ospf 1' on R1, caused R2 to learn the route shown?
exhibit:
R2# show ip route ospf
<output omitted>
Gateway of last resort is 10.1.12.1 to network 0.0.0.0

O*E2  0.0.0.0/0 [110/1] via 10.1.12.1, 00:04:12, GigabitEthernet0/0
options: default-metric 1
redistribute static subnets
default-information originate
rationales: Wrong: default-metric only sets the metric given to redistributed routes. It does not originate a default route.
Wrong: IOS does not inject a static default route into OSPF with the redistribute command. The default route needs 'default-information originate'.
Wrong: this network statement enables OSPF on every interface of R1. It does not advertise the 0.0.0.0/0 route.
Correct: this makes R1 advertise a default route into OSPF as long as it has one in its own routing table. Other routers see it as an external type 2 route (O*E2) with metric 1.
explanation: 'default-information originate' advertises 0.0.0.0/0 into OSPF when the router already has a default route (add 'always' to advertise it regardless). It appears on other routers as O*E2 with administrative distance 110.

question: R1 G0/1 has the address 172.16.5.1/24. Which two configurations each enable OSPF process 10 in area 0 on G0/1 and on no other interface? (Choose two.)
options: interface GigabitEthernet0/1, then ip ospf 10 area 0
router ospf 10, then network 172.16.4.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
interface GigabitEthernet0/1, then ip ospf area 0
router ospf 10, then network 172.16.5.1 0.0.0.0 area 0
router ospf 10, then network 172.16.5.0 0.0.0.255
rationales: Correct: the interface-level command enables the named process and area directly on G0/1, with no network statement needed.
Wrong: this range is 172.16.4.0 to 172.16.4.255, which does not contain 172.16.5.1.
Wrong: the interface command needs the process ID before the area keyword. Without it the command is rejected.
Correct: wildcard 0.0.0.0 matches exactly the address 172.16.5.1, so only G0/1 is placed in area 0 of process 10.
Wrong: the network command is incomplete without the area keyword and an area ID, so IOS rejects it.
explanation: OSPFv2 can be enabled on an interface in two ways: a matching 'network <address> <wildcard> area <id>' statement under the process, or 'ip ospf <process-id> area <id>' on the interface itself.

question: R5 is a new router that has only IPv6 addresses (no IPv4 address on any interface). IPv6 routing is enabled and 'ipv6 ospf 1 area 0' is configured on G0/0, but the OSPFv3 process does not start and logs that it could not pick a router ID. What should the engineer configure?
options: Under ipv6 router ospf 1: router-id 2001:db8::5
On G0/0: ipv6 address fe80::5 link-local
Under ipv6 router ospf 1: router-id 5.5.5.5
A loopback interface with the IPv6 address 2001:db8::5/128
rationales: Wrong: the router-id command only accepts a 32-bit value in IPv4 dotted-decimal format. An IPv6 address is rejected.
Wrong: link-local addresses are used as the source of OSPFv3 packets, but they do not provide the router ID.
Correct: OSPFv3 still uses a 32-bit router ID written in dotted decimal. With no IPv4 address to borrow, it must be set manually.
Wrong: the router ID is never derived from an IPv6 address, so an IPv6 loopback does not help.
explanation: OSPFv3 chooses its 32-bit router ID in the same way as OSPFv2: router-id command, then highest loopback IPv4 address, then highest interface IPv4 address. On an IPv6-only router you must configure router-id under 'ipv6 router ospf <pid>'.

question: R1 G0/0 (2001:db8:12::1/64) connects to R2, and R1 G0/1 (2001:db8:10::1/64) connects to a LAN. R2 is correctly configured for OSPFv3 area 0. Which configuration on R1 brings up the adjacency with R2?
exhibit:
R1# show ipv6 protocols
IPv6 Routing Protocol is "connected"
IPv6 Routing Protocol is "ND"
IPv6 Routing Protocol is "ospf 1"
  Router ID 1.1.1.1
  Number of areas: 1 normal, 0 stub, 0 nssa
  Interfaces (Area 0):
    GigabitEthernet0/1
  Redistribution:
    None

R1# show ipv6 ospf neighbor
R1#
options: interface GigabitEthernet0/0, then ipv6 ospf 1 area 0
ipv6 router ospf 1, then network 2001:db8:12::/64 area 0
ipv6 router ospf 1, then router-id 2.2.2.2
interface GigabitEthernet0/0, then ip ospf 1 area 0
rationales: Correct: only G0/1 is listed under 'Interfaces (Area 0)'. OSPFv3 is enabled per interface, so G0/0 needs 'ipv6 ospf 1 area 0' before it sends hellos to R2.
Wrong: the 'ipv6 router ospf' process has no network command. OSPFv3 interfaces are enabled in interface configuration mode.
Wrong: R1 already has a router ID (1.1.1.1). Changing it does not add G0/0 to OSPFv3, and copying a neighbour's ID could create a duplicate.
Wrong: 'ip ospf 1 area 0' enables OSPFv2 for IPv4 on the interface. It does nothing for IPv6 routing.
explanation: OSPFv3 has no network statements. Each interface is added with 'ipv6 ospf <process-id> area <area-id>'. 'show ipv6 protocols' lists the interfaces that are in each area, which makes a missing interface easy to spot.

question: R2 G0/0 has the global address 2001:db8:12::2/64 and the link-local address FE80::2. Why does R1 show FE80::2 as the next hop for the OSPF route?
exhibit:
R1# show ipv6 route ospf
<output omitted>
O   2001:DB8:20::/64 [110/2]
     via FE80::2, GigabitEthernet0/0
options: R2 is not advertising its global unicast prefix on the link into OSPFv3
The route was learned from a Router Advertisement, not from OSPFv3
R1 is missing the ipv6 unicast-routing command, so it falls back to link-local addressing
OSPFv3 sends its packets from link-local addresses, and the neighbour's link-local address is used as the next hop
rationales: Wrong: the next hop is link-local whether or not global prefixes are advertised. This is normal OSPFv3 behaviour, not a symptom of a missing prefix.
Wrong: the code O and the [110/2] distance/metric show an OSPF intra-area route. Routes from Router Advertisements are flagged ND.
Wrong: without ipv6 unicast-routing R1 could not run OSPFv3 at all, so it would have no O routes.
Correct: OSPFv3 neighbours talk to each other using link-local source addresses, and routes learned from a neighbour point at that neighbour's link-local address plus the exit interface.
explanation: IPv6 routing protocols use link-local addresses for neighbour communication, so OSPFv3 routes list a link-local next hop together with the outgoing interface. OSPFv3 keeps administrative distance 110.

question: An engineer enters 'ipv6 router ospf 1' on a newly installed router, and IOS rejects the command with a message that IPv6 routing is not enabled. Which command must be entered first?
options: ipv6 unicast-routing in global configuration mode
ipv6 enable in interface configuration mode
ipv6 address autoconfig in interface configuration mode
ip routing in global configuration mode
rationales: Correct: this global command turns on IPv6 packet forwarding and is required before any IPv6 routing protocol can be configured.
Wrong: this only enables IPv6 on one interface and gives it a link-local address. The router still does not route IPv6.
Wrong: this makes the interface obtain its own address by SLAAC, as a host would. It does not enable IPv6 routing.
Wrong: this enables IPv4 routing, which is on by default on routers and has no effect on IPv6.
explanation: IPv6 routing is off by default on IOS routers. 'ipv6 unicast-routing' must be configured globally before OSPFv3 (or IPv6 forwarding between interfaces) will work.

question: R1 G0/0 is 2001:db8:12::1/64. Because of a typing error, R2 G0/0 on the same link is 2001:db8:21::2/64. Both interfaces have 'ipv6 ospf 1 area 0', automatically generated link-local addresses, default timers and unique router IDs. What is the result?
options: The adjacency forms only after the same OSPFv3 process ID is configured on both routers
The neighbours stay in ExStart, because a prefix mismatch is treated like an MTU mismatch
The adjacency reaches FULL, because OSPFv3 forms neighbours over link-local addresses and does not compare the global prefixes
No adjacency forms, because OSPFv3 ignores hellos from a neighbour in a different prefix
rationales: Wrong: both routers already use process 1, and in any case the process ID is locally significant in OSPFv3 just as in OSPFv2.
Wrong: ExStart problems come from an MTU mismatch. The interface prefix plays no part in the database description exchange.
Correct: OSPFv3 runs per link, not per subnet. Hellos are sent from link-local addresses and carry no prefix or mask, so the differing global prefixes do not block the adjacency.
Wrong: that is OSPFv2 behaviour, where the subnet and mask must match. OSPFv3 hellos do not carry the interface prefix.
explanation: OSPFv2 requires both ends of a link to be in the same subnet with the same mask. OSPFv3 does not: it uses link-local addresses, so neighbours can be FULL even when the global addressing is wrong. Check the addressing separately when hosts cannot reach each other.

question: Match each type of OSPF traffic to the multicast address it is sent to.
pairs: OSPFv2 packets for all OSPF routers
OSPFv2 packets for the DR and BDR
OSPFv3 packets for all OSPF routers
OSPFv3 packets for the DR and BDR
explanation: OSPFv2 uses 224.0.0.5 (all OSPF routers) and 224.0.0.6 (DR and BDR). OSPFv3 uses the matching IPv6 link-local multicast groups FF02::5 and FF02::6. 224.0.0.18 is VRRP and FF02::2 is the all-routers group.

question: R2 has the addresses 192.168.10.3 on G0/0 and 192.168.20.3 on G0/1. Which two statements about the output are correct? (Choose two.)
exhibit:
R2# show standby brief
                     P indicates configured to preempt.
                     |
Interface   Grp  Pri P State   Active          Standby         Virtual IP
Gi0/0       10   100 P Standby 192.168.10.2    local           192.168.10.254
Gi0/1       20   120 P Active  local           192.168.20.2    192.168.20.254
options: Hosts in 192.168.20.0/24 must be configured with 192.168.20.3 as their default gateway
R2 currently answers ARP requests for 192.168.10.254
If the router at 192.168.10.2 fails, R2 takes over forwarding for 192.168.10.254
Hosts that use 192.168.20.254 as their default gateway currently have their traffic forwarded by R2
R2 can never become active for group 10 because its priority is only 100
rationales: Wrong: hosts use the virtual IP (192.168.20.254) as their gateway, which is the whole point of an FHRP. Using a real router address would remove the redundancy.
Wrong: R2 is Standby for group 10. Only the active router, 192.168.10.2, answers ARP for the virtual IP and forwards the traffic.
Correct: R2 is the Standby router for group 10. When hellos from the active router stop for the hold time, the standby router becomes active.
Correct: R2 is Active for group 20 (Active column shows local), so it owns the virtual IP 192.168.20.254 and forwards traffic sent to it.
Wrong: priority only decides who wins an election. A standby router takes over when the active router fails, whatever its priority.
explanation: In 'show standby brief', State shows this router's role, 'local' in the Active or Standby column means this router, and Virtual IP is the gateway address hosts use. The active router forwards; the standby router waits to take over.

question: R1 was the active router until it was reloaded for maintenance. It has now been back up for ten minutes. Which command on R1 G0/0 makes R1 the active router again?
exhibit:
R1# show standby brief
                     P indicates configured to preempt.
                     |
Interface   Grp  Pri P State   Active          Standby         Virtual IP
Gi0/0       10   150   Standby 192.168.10.3    local           192.168.10.254

R2# show standby brief
                     P indicates configured to preempt.
                     |
Interface   Grp  Pri P State   Active          Standby         Virtual IP
Gi0/0       10   100   Active  local           192.168.10.2    192.168.10.254
options: standby 10 timers 3 10
standby 10 priority 200
standby 10 track 1 decrement 60
standby 10 preempt
rationales: Wrong: 3 and 10 seconds are already the default hello and hold timers. Timers only control how quickly a failed router is detected, not who is active.
Wrong: R1 already has the higher priority. Without preemption a higher priority does not displace a router that is already active.
Wrong: tracking can only lower R1's priority when the tracked object goes down. It cannot make R1 take the active role.
Correct: there is no P in R1's output, so preemption is off (the HSRP default). With preempt enabled, R1's priority of 150 lets it take the active role back from R2 (100).
explanation: HSRP preemption is disabled by default. A router with a higher priority that comes up later stays standby unless 'standby <group> preempt' is configured on it. The P column in 'show standby brief' shows whether preempt is configured.

question: R1 is normally the active HSRP router for group 10, and both routers have preemption enabled. Why is R1 in the standby state now?
exhibit:
R1# show standby
GigabitEthernet0/0 - Group 10
  State is Standby
    4 state changes, last state change 00:02:41
  Virtual IP address is 192.168.10.254
  Active virtual MAC address is 0000.0c07.ac0a (MAC Not In Use)
    Local virtual MAC address is 0000.0c07.ac0a (v1 default)
  Hello time 3 sec, hold time 10 sec
    Next hello sent in 1.264 secs
  Preemption enabled
  Active router is 192.168.10.3, priority 100 (expires in 9.136 sec)
  Standby router is local
  Priority 95 (configured 110)
    Track object 1 state Down decrement 15
  Group name is "hsrp-Gi0/0-10" (default)
options: R1's hello and hold timers have been changed from the defaults and no longer match
R1 is not configured to preempt, so it cannot take the active role back
The other router has the higher IP address, which wins the HSRP election
A tracked object went down and lowered R1's priority to 95, below the other router's 100
rationales: Wrong: 3 seconds hello and 10 seconds hold are the HSRP defaults, and R1 is clearly still hearing the active router's hellos.
Wrong: the output says 'Preemption enabled'. R1 will take the role back once its priority is higher than 100 again.
Wrong: the IP address is only a tie-breaker when priorities are equal. Here the priorities are 95 and 100.
Correct: the configured priority is 110, but track object 1 is Down with a decrement of 15, giving 95. The other router (priority 100, preempt enabled) therefore took over.
explanation: HSRP tracking lowers a router's priority when a tracked object (for example an uplink) goes down. If the new priority drops below a peer that has preempt enabled, the peer becomes active. 'Priority 95 (configured 110)' is the clue.

question: R1 and R2 are powered on at the same time with the configuration shown. Which router becomes the active HSRP router, and why?
exhibit:
R1# show running-config interface GigabitEthernet0/0
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 192.168.10.2 255.255.255.0
 standby 10 ip 192.168.10.254

R2# show running-config interface GigabitEthernet0/0
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 192.168.10.3 255.255.255.0
 standby 10 ip 192.168.10.254
options: R2, because both use the default priority of 100 and the highest interface IP address breaks the tie
Both routers, because HSRP shares the load between routers with equal priority
Neither router, because a priority must be configured before a router can become active
R1, because both use the default priority of 100 and the lowest interface IP address breaks the tie
rationales: Correct: no priority is configured, so both use 100. With equal priorities the router with the highest IP address on the HSRP interface (192.168.10.3) wins.
Wrong: an HSRP group has one active router. The other router is standby and does not forward traffic for the virtual IP.
Wrong: the priority defaults to 100 when it is not configured, so an election still takes place.
Wrong: the default priority is right, but the tie is broken by the highest IP address, not the lowest.
explanation: HSRP elects the active router by highest priority (default 100), then highest interface IP address. The loser becomes the standby router.

question: An HSRP group with a virtual IP address is configured on a router interface. Put the HSRP states in the order the router passes through them on its way to forwarding traffic for the group, starting with the first.
explanation: Initial: HSRP is not yet running. Listen: the router knows the virtual IP and listens for hellos. Speak: it sends hellos and takes part in the election. Standby: it is the backup candidate. Active: it forwards traffic sent to the virtual IP and MAC. (A Learn state exists only when the router does not yet know the virtual IP.)

question: Match each first hop redundancy group to the virtual MAC address it uses.
explanation: HSRPv1 uses 0000.0c07.acXX and HSRPv2 uses 0000.0c9f.fXXX, where the X digits are the group number in hexadecimal (10 = 0a, 300 = 12c). VRRP for IPv4 uses 0000.5e00.01XX. The two unused addresses come from writing group 10 as '10' without converting it to hex.

question: No VRRP priority command is configured on R1. Why does R1 show a priority of 255?
exhibit:
R1# show vrrp brief
Interface          Grp Pri Time  Own Pre State   Master addr     Group addr
Gi0/0              1   255 3003   Y   Y  Master  192.168.1.1     192.168.1.1
options: 255 is the default VRRP priority
R1 is the IP address owner: the group's virtual IP is the real address of its G0/0 interface
R1 has the highest interface IP address on the segment, so VRRP raised its priority
A master advertises priority 255 when it is about to give up the master role
rationales: Wrong: the default VRRP priority is 100. Configurable priorities run from 1 to 254.
Correct: the Group addr equals R1's own address and the Own column shows Y. The address owner automatically uses priority 255 and is the master whenever it is up.
Wrong: the IP address is only a tie-breaker between routers with equal priority. It never changes the priority value.
Wrong: a master that is giving up its role advertises priority 0, not 255.
explanation: VRRP allows the virtual IP to be a real interface address. The router that owns that address gets priority 255 automatically and always becomes master when it is available. HSRP does not allow this; its virtual IP must be a separate address.

question: R1 (priority 120) and R2 (priority 100) run VRRP group 1 with all other settings at their defaults. R1 fails and R2 becomes master. R1 then comes back online. What happens?
options: R1 and R2 both act as master and share the traffic
R2 remains master, because the router that has been master longest is preferred
R2 remains master until it fails, because preemption must be configured manually
R1 becomes master again, because VRRP preemption is enabled by default
rationales: Wrong: a VRRP group has one master. The other routers are backups and do not forward for the virtual IP.
Wrong: VRRP does not consider how long a router has been master. Priority decides, and preemption is on.
Wrong: that describes HSRP, where preemption is off by default. In VRRP it is on by default.
Correct: VRRP preempts by default, so the higher-priority R1 takes the master role back as soon as it returns.
explanation: Preemption is the key default difference: VRRP has it enabled, HSRP has it disabled. With defaults, a recovered higher-priority VRRP router takes over again; a recovered HSRP router does not.

question: Which two statements about VRRP are true? (Choose two.)
options: The master sends advertisements every 1 second by default
It is an open standard, so routers from different vendors can share a group
The forwarding router is called the active router and its backup is the standby router
Hellos are sent every 3 seconds with a 10-second hold time by default
Its IPv4 virtual MAC address begins with 0000.0c07.ac
rationales: Correct: the default VRRP advertisement interval is 1 second.
Correct: VRRP is defined by the IETF (RFC 5798 for version 3) and is not tied to one vendor.
Wrong: active and standby are HSRP terms. VRRP uses master and backup.
Wrong: 3 seconds hello and 10 seconds hold are the HSRP defaults, not VRRP's.
Wrong: 0000.0c07.acXX is the HSRP version 1 virtual MAC. VRRP for IPv4 uses 0000.5e00.01XX.
explanation: VRRP: open standard, master/backup, 1-second advertisements, preemption on, virtual MAC 0000.5e00.01XX. HSRP: Cisco proprietary, active/standby, 3-second hello and 10-second hold, preemption off.

question: R1 and R2 are in the same VLAN and are configured for the same VRRP group. The outputs are taken at the same time. What do they indicate?
exhibit:
R1# show vrrp brief
Interface          Grp Pri Time  Own Pre State   Master addr     Group addr
Gi0/0              1   120 3531       Y  Master  192.168.1.2     192.168.1.254

R2# show vrrp brief
Interface          Grp Pri Time  Own Pre State   Master addr     Group addr
Gi0/0              1   100 3609       Y  Master  192.168.1.3     192.168.1.254
options: R1 and R2 are not receiving each other's VRRP advertisements, so each believes it is the only router in the group
Both routers have preemption enabled, which makes each of them claim the master role
This is normal, because VRRP uses two masters to share the load for one group
R2 preempted R1 because R2 has the higher interface IP address
rationales: Correct: a backup only becomes master when it stops hearing a master with a higher priority. Two masters for one group means the advertisements are not getting through, for example because of a Layer 2 fault or a filter between the routers.
Wrong: preemption only allows a higher-priority router to replace a lower-priority master. It does not produce two masters.
Wrong: one VRRP group has exactly one master. Sharing load needs several groups with different masters.
Wrong: R1 has the higher priority (120 against 100), and the IP address is only compared when priorities are equal. R1 also still shows Master.
explanation: Each router lists itself as the master address for the same group address. In VRRP (and HSRP) two forwarding routers for one group means they cannot hear each other, so check the Layer 2 path, VLAN assignment and any ACLs between them.

question: A router does not use AAA, and its vty lines are configured with login local. An engineer wants a local account named netadmin that is placed straight into privileged EXEC mode at login and whose password is stored in the configuration as a one-way hash. Which command meets both requirements?
options: username netadmin privilege 15 password Str0ngPass!
username netadmin secret Str0ngPass!
username netadmin privilege 15 secret Str0ngPass!
enable secret Str0ngPass!
rationales: Wrong: privilege 15 is right, but the password keyword does not store a one-way hash. The password is kept as clear text, or as weak, reversible type 7 if service password-encryption is enabled.
Wrong: the secret keyword stores a hash, but without the privilege keyword the account gets the default privilege level 1, so the user lands in user EXEC mode.
Correct: privilege 15 places the user directly in privileged EXEC mode, and the secret keyword stores the password as a one-way hash.
Wrong: enable secret sets the hashed password for entering privileged EXEC mode with the enable command. It does not create a user account.
explanation: Use username NAME privilege 15 secret PASSWORD for a local administrator: privilege sets the level given at login, and secret (not password) stores a one-way hash.

question: Refer to the exhibit. A user at the R1> prompt types enable. Which password does R1 accept?
exhibit:
R1# show running-config | include enable
enable secret 9 $9$nu0TzQ5lXwPb3k$Y8rZc1mE4qGdT7uWv2JxKp9LsB6hN0aFoRiCyD3eM5t
enable password Lab123
options: Only Lab123, because the most recently listed enable command takes effect
Only the password that was hashed by the enable secret command
Either Lab123 or the enable secret password
Both passwords, entered one after the other
rationales: Wrong: the order of the two lines does not matter. When an enable secret exists, the enable password is not used at all.
Correct: when both commands are configured, IOS uses the enable secret and ignores the enable password.
Wrong: the two are not alternatives. The enable password is only used when no enable secret is configured.
Wrong: IOS prompts once. Only the enable secret is checked when it is configured.
explanation: If enable secret and enable password are both present, the enable secret wins and the enable password is ignored. Always use enable secret, which is stored as a hash.

question: Refer to the exhibit. An engineer can log in to R1 with Telnet using a local account, but every SSH attempt fails immediately, before any password prompt appears. Which change fixes the problem and leaves SSH as the only way to reach the vty lines?
exhibit:
R1# show ip ssh | include version
SSH Enabled - version 2.0
R1# show running-config | section line vty
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input telnet
options: Enter ip ssh version 2 in global configuration mode
Enter crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048 in global configuration mode
Enter transport input ssh under line vty 0 4
Enter login under line vty 0 4
Enter transport output ssh under line vty 0 4
rationales: Wrong: the output already shows SSH enabled at version 2.0. The version is not what is blocking the session.
Wrong: SSH is reported as enabled, which means an RSA key pair already exists. New keys would not make the vty lines accept SSH.
Correct: transport input telnet allows only Telnet on the vty lines. transport input ssh replaces it, so the lines accept SSH and refuse Telnet.
Wrong: login makes the lines check a line password instead of the local user database. It does not change which protocols the lines accept.
Wrong: transport output controls the protocols a user on that line may use for outgoing sessions from R1. Incoming sessions are controlled by transport input.
explanation: The SSH server can be running and still be unreachable: transport input on the vty lines decides which protocols may connect. Use transport input ssh to allow SSH only.

question: A new router already has a hostname, a domain name and a local user account. AAA is not enabled. The engineer must make the vty lines accept SSH but not Telnet, and check logins against the local user database. Which three commands are needed? (Choose three.)
options: crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
login
transport input ssh
transport output ssh
login local
ip http secure-server
rationales: Correct: the SSH server needs an RSA key pair. Generating the keys is what enables SSH on the router.
Wrong: login on its own makes the line ask for the line password set with the password command. It does not use the local username database.
Correct: under line vty this allows incoming SSH sessions only, so Telnet is refused.
Wrong: this limits the protocols used for sessions started from the router. It has no effect on incoming management sessions.
Correct: under line vty this makes the router check the username and password against the local user database.
Wrong: this enables the HTTPS server used for web-based management. It has nothing to do with SSH access to the vty lines.
explanation: SSH needs a hostname, a domain name and an RSA key pair (crypto key generate rsa). On the vty lines, login local selects the local user database and transport input ssh blocks Telnet.

question: Refer to the exhibit. The TACACS+ server at 10.10.10.5 is reachable and is answering requests. An engineer connects to R1 and logs in as rescue with the correct local password. The account rescue does not exist on the TACACS+ server. What is the result?
exhibit:
R1# show running-config | section aaa|username|tacacs
aaa new-model
aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local
aaa session-id common
username rescue privilege 15 secret 5 $1$v3Kp$Qm0zT8yC1uXwLr5eNfA9B/
tacacs server TAC1
 address ipv4 10.10.10.5
 key 7 0822455D0A16
options: The login succeeds, because R1 tries the local database after the server rejects the user
The login succeeds, because local usernames are always checked before any server group
The login is refused, because the server answered with a reject and the local method is therefore never tried
The login succeeds, but at privilege level 1 because the server did not authorise level 15
rationales: Wrong: a reject from the server is a final answer. R1 moves to the next method only when the current method returns an error, such as no response from the server.
Wrong: methods are tried strictly in the order listed. Here group tacacs+ comes first and local second.
Correct: the server is working and does not know the user, so it rejects the login. The local method is a fallback only for when the TACACS+ servers do not respond.
Wrong: authentication fails outright, so no session is created at any privilege level.
explanation: In a method list, the next method is used only if the previous one fails to respond (error or timeout). A reject from a working server ends the attempt, so the local account is a fallback for server outages only.

question: Which two statements describe RADIUS? (Choose two.)
options: It uses TCP port 49
It uses UDP, with port 1812 for authentication and port 1813 for accounting
It encrypts the whole body of every packet
It encrypts only the password in an access request and sends the rest in clear text
It handles authentication and authorisation as two separate exchanges
rationales: Wrong: TCP port 49 is used by TACACS+. RADIUS runs over UDP.
Correct: these are the standard RADIUS ports, and RADIUS uses UDP as its transport.
Wrong: that is TACACS+ behaviour. RADIUS protects only the password field.
Correct: RADIUS hides the user password attribute, while other attributes such as the username travel unencrypted.
Wrong: RADIUS combines them, returning authorisation attributes in the same reply that accepts the authentication. Separating the functions is a TACACS+ feature.
explanation: RADIUS: open standard, UDP 1812 (authentication and authorisation combined) and UDP 1813 (accounting), only the password encrypted. TACACS+: TCP 49, whole payload encrypted, the three functions separated.

question: A network team wants each command that an administrator types on the routers to be checked against a central policy before it runs, independently of the check that was made at login. Which protocol should the routers use as AAA clients, and why?
options: RADIUS, because it treats authentication, authorisation and accounting as separate functions
TACACS+, because it uses UDP, which keeps per-command checks fast
RADIUS, because it is the Cisco-developed protocol designed for device administration
TACACS+, because it separates authentication, authorisation and accounting, so each command can be authorised on its own
rationales: Wrong: RADIUS combines authentication and authorisation in one exchange, which makes it poorly suited to authorising individual commands.
Wrong: TACACS+ is the right protocol, but the reason is false. TACACS+ uses TCP port 49.
Wrong: RADIUS is an open standard used mainly for network access such as 802.1X and VPN logins. The Cisco-developed protocol for device administration is TACACS+.
Correct: TACACS+ keeps the three functions separate, so the router can send an authorisation request for every command after the user has logged in.
explanation: TACACS+ separates authentication, authorisation and accounting, which allows per-command authorisation and makes it the usual choice for device administration. RADIUS combines authentication and authorisation and is typical for network access.

question: Match each AAA term to its description.
pairs: Verifies the identity of the user, for example with a username and password
Decides what an identified user is permitted to do
Records what the user did and when, for audit purposes
The router or switch that passes the user's credentials to the AAA server
The ordered set of sources a device tries when it performs an AAA function
distractors: Encrypts user data as it crosses the network
explanation: Authentication asks who you are, authorisation asks what you may do, and accounting records what you did. The network device is the AAA client of the TACACS+ or RADIUS server, and a method list (for example group tacacs+ local) sets the order in which sources are tried. AAA does not encrypt user data.

question: A switch is a TACACS+ client configured for login authentication, EXEC authorisation and EXEC accounting. Put the events in the order in which they occur when an administrator opens an SSH session to the switch.
items: The administrator connects to the switch and supplies a username and password
The switch sends the credentials to the TACACS+ server over TCP port 49
The server checks the credentials and replies that authentication has passed
The switch asks the server whether the user may start an EXEC session and receives the permitted privilege level
The switch sends the server an accounting start record for the session
explanation: The order follows the three As. The switch (AAA client) first relays the credentials to the server for authentication, then requests authorisation for the EXEC session, and only then begins accounting for the session that has been started.

question: A security audit finds that router configurations are backed up with TFTP. Which statement correctly explains why SCP or SFTP is the better choice?
options: SCP and SFTP both run over SSH on TCP port 22, so the login is authenticated and the file is encrypted in transit; TFTP uses UDP port 69 and offers neither
SCP and SFTP are FTP with TLS encryption added, and use TCP ports 20 and 21
TFTP authenticates with a username and password but sends the file in clear text, so SCP and SFTP only add encryption
SCP and SFTP use UDP port 22, which is faster than the TCP transport used by TFTP
rationales: Correct: both protocols use the SSH transport, which provides authentication and encryption. TFTP has no login and sends the file in clear text over UDP port 69.
Wrong: FTP protected by TLS is FTPS. SCP and SFTP are not based on FTP; they run inside an SSH session on TCP port 22.
Wrong: TFTP has no authentication at all. Anyone who can reach the server can request a file.
Wrong: the transports are the other way round. SSH, and therefore SCP and SFTP, uses TCP port 22, and TFTP uses UDP port 69.
explanation: SCP and SFTP ride on SSH (TCP 22), so transfers are authenticated and encrypted. TFTP (UDP 69) has no authentication and no encryption, and FTP sends credentials in clear text.

question: An engineer must back up the running configuration of R1 to a file named R1-confg on the server 192.0.2.50, using SCP and the server account backup. Which command does this?
options: copy scp://backup@192.0.2.50/R1-confg running-config
copy running-config tftp://192.0.2.50/R1-confg
scp running-config backup@192.0.2.50:R1-confg
copy running-config scp://backup@192.0.2.50/R1-confg
rationales: Wrong: copy takes the source first and the destination second. This command fetches the file from the server and merges it into the running configuration.
Wrong: this sends the file with TFTP, which has no authentication or encryption, and it does not use the backup account.
Wrong: this is the syntax of a Linux scp client. On IOS XE, file transfers are made with the copy command and a URL.
Correct: the source is running-config and the destination is an SCP URL in the form scp://user@host/filename. IOS then prompts for the password.
explanation: The IOS copy command is always copy SOURCE DESTINATION. A remote SCP location is written as scp://username@host/filename.

question: An engineer wants to push a new IOS XE image from a laptop to R1 with an SCP client, so R1 must act as the SCP server. Which two items must be in place on R1? (Choose two.)
options: The ip scp server enable command in global configuration mode
The tftp-server command, pointing at the file in flash
A working SSH server, with an RSA key pair and vty lines that accept SSH
The ip ftp username and ip ftp password commands
The ip http secure-server command
rationales: Correct: the SCP server function is disabled by default and is switched on with this command.
Wrong: tftp-server makes the router offer a file to TFTP clients. It has no connection with SCP.
Correct: SCP is carried inside an SSH session, so SSH must already work on R1 and the user must be able to authenticate.
Wrong: these set the credentials that the router itself presents when it acts as an FTP client.
Wrong: this enables the HTTPS server for web management. SCP does not use HTTPS.
explanation: For a router to be an SCP server, SSH must be working (keys, vty access and a user that can authenticate with sufficient privilege, normally level 15) and ip scp server enable must be configured.

question: Refer to the exhibit. After copying a new image to R1 with SCP, the engineer runs the command shown. The MD5 value published for this image on the Cisco software download page is different from the value in the output. What should the engineer conclude?
options: The difference is expected, because SCP encrypts the file and the stored copy therefore hashes differently
The file in flash is not identical to the original, so it should be deleted and transferred again before it is used
The difference is expected, because each router mixes its serial number into the hash
The image is good, because verify /md5 only proves that the file can be read and its result changes on every run
rationales: Wrong: SCP encrypts the data only while it is in transit. The file written to flash should be identical, byte for byte, to the original.
Correct: an MD5 mismatch means the contents differ from the published file, because of corruption, an incomplete copy or tampering. The router must not be booted from it.
Wrong: the hash is calculated from the file contents only. The same file gives the same MD5 value on every device.
Wrong: an MD5 hash is deterministic. Its whole purpose here is to be compared with the published value.
explanation: Run verify /md5 on a transferred image and compare the result with the published hash. Any mismatch means the file is not the genuine, complete image: delete it and copy it again.

question: An engineer is upgrading a router that boots from a single image file in flash. The new image is on an SCP server. Put the tasks in the recommended order.
items: Run dir flash: to confirm that there is enough free space for the new image
Copy the image from the server with copy scp: flash:
Run verify /md5 on the copied file and compare the result with the published hash
Use the boot system command to point the router at the new image file
Save the change with copy running-config startup-config
explanation: Check free space before copying, and verify the hash before relying on the file. The boot system command is read from the startup configuration at boot, so it must be saved before the reload that activates the new image.

question: Match each NAT address term to its description.
pairs: The address configured on a host in the internal network, usually a private address
The address that represents an internal host to the outside network, usually a public address
The address assigned to an external host by its owner, as it is routed on the outside network
The address of an external host as it appears to hosts on the inside network
distractors: The address of the next-hop router used by the NAT device
explanation: Inside or outside says where the host is. Local or global says where the address is seen: local addresses are seen from the inside network and global addresses from the outside network. With ordinary source NAT the outside local and outside global addresses are the same.

question: An internal web server at 10.1.1.10 must always be reachable from the Internet as 203.0.113.10. Which command creates this one-to-one translation?
options: ip nat inside source static 203.0.113.10 10.1.1.10
ip nat inside source static 10.1.1.10 203.0.113.10
ip nat outside source static 10.1.1.10 203.0.113.10
ip nat inside source list 10 interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1 overload
rationales: Wrong: the addresses are reversed. The syntax is inside local first, then inside global.
Correct: this permanently maps the inside local address 10.1.1.10 to the inside global address 203.0.113.10, so sessions can also be started from the outside.
Wrong: ip nat outside source translates the source address of packets that arrive on the outside interface. It is not used to publish an inside server.
Wrong: this is PAT. Entries are created only when an inside host sends traffic, so nothing permanent exists for sessions that start on the Internet.
explanation: Static NAT is ip nat inside source static INSIDE-LOCAL INSIDE-GLOBAL. The entry is always in the table, so outside hosts can open sessions to the inside host.
