question: R1 has its NAT inside and outside interfaces assigned, a pool created with ip nat pool PUBLIC 203.0.113.9 203.0.113.14 netmask 255.255.255.248, and ACL 1, which permits the inside subnet. Each inside host that goes online must receive its own address from the pool, with no port translation. Which command completes the configuration?
options: ip nat inside source list 1 pool PUBLIC overload
ip nat outside source list 1 pool PUBLIC
ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1 overload
ip nat inside source list 1 pool PUBLIC
rationales: Wrong: overload turns this into PAT, where many hosts share one pool address and are told apart by port number.
Wrong: ip nat outside source translates the source address of packets arriving from the outside network, not of the inside hosts.
Wrong: this ignores the pool and translates every host to the address of the interface using PAT.
Correct: this binds the ACL to the pool. Each inside local address matched by ACL 1 is given one free pool address for as long as its translation exists.
explanation: Dynamic NAT needs three parts: an ACL that matches the inside local addresses, a pool of inside global addresses, and ip nat inside source list ACL pool NAME to join them. Adding overload makes it PAT.

question: Refer to the exhibit, which shows part of the configuration of R1. All LAN hosts must share the address of the ISP-facing interface when they access the Internet. Which two commands complete the configuration? (Choose two.)
exhibit:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0
 description LAN
 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
 ip nat inside
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1
 description ISP
 ip address 203.0.113.2 255.255.255.252
!
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.1
access-list 1 permit 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255
options: ip nat inside under interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1
ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1 overload in global configuration mode
ip nat outside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1 overload in global configuration mode
ip nat outside under interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1
ip nat inside source static 192.168.10.1 203.0.113.2 in global configuration mode
rationales: Wrong: GigabitEthernet0/0/1 faces the ISP, so it is the outside interface. Marking both interfaces as inside leaves NAT with no outside interface.
Correct: this translates the sources matched by ACL 1 to the address of GigabitEthernet0/0/1, and overload lets all hosts share it by using different ports.
Wrong: the hosts to be translated are on the inside, so the statement must be ip nat inside source.
Correct: NAT needs an outside interface as well as an inside one. The ISP-facing interface has no NAT role in the exhibit.
Wrong: this is a static one-to-one mapping for the router's own LAN address. It does nothing for the hosts on the LAN.
explanation: PAT on the interface address needs ip nat inside and ip nat outside on the right interfaces, an ACL matching the inside local addresses, and ip nat inside source list ACL interface OUTSIDE-INTERFACE overload.

question: Refer to the exhibit. A reply from the web server arrives on the outside interface of R1, addressed to 203.0.113.2, TCP port 1024. What does R1 do with the packet?
options: It changes the destination to 10.1.1.11, port 51514, and forwards the packet
It changes the destination to 10.1.1.12, port 1024, and forwards the packet
It changes the destination to 10.1.1.12, port 51514, and forwards the packet
It drops the packet, because two inside hosts used the same source port and R1 cannot tell them apart
rationales: Wrong: 10.1.1.11 owns the entry whose inside global port is 51514. The packet in question is addressed to port 1024.
Wrong: PAT translates the port as well as the address. The inside local port in the matching entry is 51514, not 1024.
Correct: the entry with inside global 203.0.113.2:1024 has inside local 10.1.1.12:51514, so R1 rewrites both the destination address and the destination port.
Wrong: PAT handles this case by giving the second host a different inside global port (1024), which keeps every entry unique.
explanation: With PAT, each translation is identified by the inside global address and port. Return traffic is matched on that pair and both the address and the port are restored to the inside local values.

question: Refer to the exhibit, which shows the relevant configuration of R1. LAN hosts can ping 192.168.10.1 but cannot reach any Internet address, and show ip nat translations returns no entries. What is the cause?
exhibit:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0
 description LAN
 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
 ip nat outside
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1
 description ISP
 ip address 203.0.113.2 255.255.255.252
 ip nat inside
!
ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1 overload
ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.1
access-list 1 permit 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255
options: The wildcard mask in ACL 1 does not match the LAN subnet
The inside and outside roles are reversed: the LAN interface needs ip nat inside and the ISP interface needs ip nat outside
The overload keyword cannot be combined with an interface, so a NAT pool is required
The NAT statement should name GigabitEthernet0/0/0, the interface that the hosts connect to
rationales: Wrong: 192.168.10.0 with wildcard 0.0.0.255 matches exactly the /24 configured on the LAN interface.

Correct: ip nat inside source translates packets that enter an inside interface and leave through an outside interface. Traffic from the LAN arrives on an interface marked outside, so it is never translated.
Wrong: translating to an interface address with overload is the standard PAT configuration.
Wrong: the interface named in the statement supplies the inside global address, so it must be the Internet-facing interface, as configured.
explanation: For ip nat inside source, traffic must enter an interface marked ip nat inside and leave through one marked ip nat outside. If the roles are swapped, no translations are created.

question: Refer to the exhibit, which shows the relevant configuration of R1. VLAN 20 was added last week. Hosts in VLAN 10 use the Internet normally. Hosts in VLAN 20 can ping 192.168.20.1 and hosts in VLAN 10, but cannot reach the Internet. Which change fixes the problem?
exhibit:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0.10
 encapsulation dot1Q 10
 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
 ip nat inside
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0.20
 encapsulation dot1Q 20
 ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
 ip nat inside
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1
 ip address 203.0.113.2 255.255.255.252
 ip nat outside
!
ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1 overload
access-list 1 permit 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255
options: Add ip nat outside to interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0.20
Replace the ACL entry with access-list 1 permit 192.168.10.0 0.0.1.255
Add ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0.20 overload
Add access-list 1 permit 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255
rationales: Wrong: VLAN 20 is an inside network and its subinterface is already marked ip nat inside, which is correct.
Wrong: wildcard 0.0.1.255 matches 192.168.10.0 to 192.168.11.255 only. It still does not include 192.168.20.0/24.
Wrong: the interface in the statement supplies the public address, so it must stay as the outside interface. ACL 1 would also still not match VLAN 20.
Correct: ACL 1 selects the inside local addresses to translate and currently permits only 192.168.10.0/24. Once 192.168.20.0/24 is permitted, VLAN 20 traffic is translated.
explanation: The ACL in ip nat inside source list identifies the inside local addresses that are translated. When a new inside subnet is added, the NAT ACL must be extended to match it.

question: Refer to the exhibit. About 40 hosts on the inside LAN use R1 to reach the Internet. Six of them work, and the others cannot connect until one of the six has been idle for a long time. Which change lets all the hosts work at the same time without obtaining more public addresses?
exhibit:
R1# show ip nat statistics
Total active translations: 31 (0 static, 31 dynamic; 25 extended)
Outside interfaces:
  GigabitEthernet0/0/1
Inside interfaces:
  GigabitEthernet0/0/0
Hits: 48211  Misses: 208
Expired translations: 29
Dynamic mappings:
-- Inside Source
[Id: 1] access-list 1 pool PUBLIC refcount 31
 pool PUBLIC: id 1, netmask 255.255.255.248
        start 203.0.113.9 end 203.0.113.14
        type generic, total addresses 6, allocated 6 (100%), misses 173
options: Replace the NAT statement with ip nat inside source list 1 pool PUBLIC overload
Run clear ip nat translation * on R1
Change ACL 1 to permit any source address
Change the netmask of the pool to 255.255.255.240
rationales: Correct: the pool has six addresses and all six are allocated one-to-one. With overload, R1 performs PAT, so many hosts share each pool address by using different ports.
Wrong: this frees the six addresses only for a moment. The next six hosts to send traffic take them and the pool is exhausted again.
Wrong: the hosts are already being matched. The pool misses show that translations are being attempted and failing because no address is free.
Wrong: the netmask does not add addresses. The pool would still run from 203.0.113.9 to 203.0.113.14, which is six addresses.
explanation: Dynamic NAT without overload is one-to-one, so a pool of six addresses serves only six hosts at a time (allocated 100%, pool misses rising). Adding overload enables PAT and removes the limit.

question: An engineer needs to change the address range of the dynamic NAT pool PUBLIC. The command no ip nat pool PUBLIC is rejected with the message %Pool PUBLIC in use, cannot destroy. Which command removes the existing dynamic translations so that the pool can be deleted?
options: clear ip nat statistics
clear access-list counters 1
show ip nat translations verbose
clear ip nat translation *
rationales: Wrong: this resets the NAT counters, such as hits and misses. The translation entries stay in the table.
Wrong: this resets the match counters of the ACL. It has no effect on the NAT table.
Wrong: this only displays the entries, with extra detail such as their age. It removes nothing.
Correct: this removes all dynamic entries from the NAT table, which releases the pool addresses. Static entries are not removed.
explanation: clear ip nat translation * flushes all dynamic NAT entries. It is needed before a pool or dynamic rule that is in use can be changed; clear ip nat statistics only zeroes counters.

question: R1 is configured with ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1 overload and access-list 1 permit 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255. The NAT inside and outside interfaces are assigned correctly and no ACL is applied to any interface. A host at 192.168.30.5, on another inside subnet, sends a packet through R1 towards the Internet. What does R1 do with the packet?
options: It drops the packet because of the implicit deny at the end of ACL 1
It routes the packet without changing the source address
It translates the source to the address of GigabitEthernet0/0/1, because overload applies to all traffic from inside interfaces
It returns an ICMP administratively prohibited message to the host
rationales: Wrong: ACL 1 is not applied to an interface as a filter. Here it only selects which sources are translated, so a deny does not drop anything.
Correct: the source does not match a permit entry in the NAT ACL, so the packet is not translated. It is still routed normally, with its original source address.
Wrong: only sources permitted by the ACL in the NAT statement are translated. The overload keyword does not widen that selection.
Wrong: that is the behaviour of an ACL that filters traffic on an interface. A NAT ACL does not filter.
explanation: In a NAT statement the ACL is a classifier, not a filter: permit means translate, and deny (including the implicit deny) means forward without translation.

question: Match each DNS record type to what it does.
pairs: Maps a hostname to an IPv4 address
Maps a hostname to an IPv6 address
Makes one name an alias of another, canonical name
Names a mail server that accepts mail for a domain, with a preference value
Names an authoritative name server for a zone
Maps an IP address back to a hostname for reverse lookups
distractors: Holds free-form text, such as a domain verification string
explanation: A and AAAA give addresses (IPv4 and IPv6). CNAME is an alias to another name. MX points to the mail server name for a domain. NS lists the authoritative servers and is how zones are delegated. PTR is the reverse mapping from address to name. Free-form text is held in a TXT record.

question: A PC needs to resolve www.example.com and no DNS information is cached anywhere. Put the steps of the lookup in the order in which they occur.
items: The PC sends a query for www.example.com to its configured recursive resolver on UDP port 53
The resolver queries a root server, which refers it to the name servers for the com zone
The resolver queries a com name server, which refers it to the servers listed in the NS records for example.com
The resolver queries an authoritative server for example.com, which returns the A record
The resolver caches the answer for the TTL of the record and returns it to the PC
explanation: The client asks only its recursive resolver. The resolver follows NS delegations down the tree, from the root to com to example.com, receives the answer from an authoritative server, caches it for the TTL and replies to the client. A missing or wrong NS delegation breaks the chain for the whole zone. DNS queries normally use UDP port 53; TCP port 53 is used for zone transfers and for responses too large for UDP.

question: Refer to the exhibit. The server mail1 has been shut down for maintenance. External senders report that mail for example.com is now queued and not delivered, although the backup mail server is running at 192.0.2.26. Which two statements are correct? (Choose two.)
exhibit:
$ dig example.com MX +noall +answer
example.com.        3600  IN  MX  10 mail1.example.com.
example.com.        3600  IN  MX  20 mail2.example.com.
$ dig mail1.example.com A +noall +answer
mail1.example.com.  3600  IN  A   192.0.2.25
$ dig mail2.example.com A +noall +answer
$ dig mail2.example.com AAAA +noall +answer
$
options: When both servers are available, senders try mail2 first because 20 is the higher preference
Senders cannot use mail2, because mail2.example.com has no A or AAAA record
The MX records are faulty, because an MX record must contain an IP address rather than a hostname
In normal operation mail1 is tried first, because the lower preference value has the higher priority
Senders need a PTR record for 192.0.2.26 before they can find mail2
rationales: Wrong: the lowest preference value is the most preferred, so mail1 (10) is tried before mail2 (20).
Correct: an MX record gives only a hostname. The sender must then resolve that name to an address, and both lookups for mail2 return nothing.
Wrong: an MX record must point to a hostname. The address comes from that host's A or AAAA record.
Correct: 10 is lower than 20, so mail1 is the primary and mail2 is used only when mail1 cannot be reached.
Wrong: a PTR record maps an address back to a name. Senders locate a mail server with the MX record and then the A or AAAA record of its target.
explanation: Mail delivery needs an MX record for the domain and an A or AAAA record for each MX target. The lowest MX preference value is tried first; a backup MX whose name does not resolve is useless.

question: Refer to the exhibit. R1 can reach the web server by address but not by name. R1 must resolve hostnames by querying the DNS server at 192.0.2.53. Which two commands are needed? (Choose two.)
exhibit:
R1# ping 192.0.2.80
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 5, 100-byte ICMP Echos to 192.0.2.80, timeout is 2 seconds:
!!!!!
Success rate is 100 percent (5/5), round-trip min/avg/max = 1/2/4 ms
R1# ping www.example.com
Translating "www.example.com"
% Unrecognized host or address, or protocol not running.

R1# show running-config | include domain|name-server
no ip domain lookup
ip domain name example.com
options: ip name-server 192.0.2.53
ip dns server
ip host www.example.com 192.0.2.80
ip domain lookup
ip helper-address 192.0.2.53
rationales: Correct: this tells R1 which DNS server to query. The filtered output shows that no name server is configured.
Wrong: this makes R1 itself answer DNS queries from other devices. It does not make R1 send its own queries to 192.0.2.53.
Wrong: this adds one static entry to the local host table of R1. It does not use the DNS server and resolves only that single name.
Correct: the configuration contains no ip domain lookup, which switches off DNS resolution on R1. This command switches it back on.
Wrong: this interface command relays broadcasts, such as DHCP requests from clients, to a server. It plays no part in name resolution by the router.
explanation: An IOS XE device resolves names through DNS only if ip domain lookup is enabled (the default) and at least one ip name-server is configured. Working pings by address with failing pings by name point at name resolution, not routing.

question: Refer to the exhibit. A web server was moved from 192.0.2.80 to 192.0.2.90, and the A record on the authoritative server ns1.example.com was updated about seven hours ago. Users of the corporate resolver 10.1.1.53 are still sent to the old address. What explains the output?
exhibit:
$ dig @ns1.example.com www.example.com A +noall +answer
www.example.com.    86400  IN  A  192.0.2.90
$ dig @10.1.1.53 www.example.com A +noall +answer
www.example.com.    61370  IN  A  192.0.2.80
options: The authoritative server still holds the old record, so the zone must be edited again
A CNAME record must be created before the address in an A record can be changed
The resolver is answering from its cache and will keep the old record until the remaining TTL, about 17 hours, has counted down
The resolver rejects the new A record because no PTR record exists for 192.0.2.90
rationales: Wrong: the first query, sent straight to ns1.example.com, returns the new address 192.0.2.90.
Wrong: an A record can be changed directly. A CNAME is an alias to another name and is not involved here.
Correct: the resolver cached the old record with a TTL of 86400 seconds (24 hours). The TTL has counted down to 61370 seconds, so the old answer is served for roughly another 17 hours.
Wrong: forward lookups do not depend on PTR records. A missing PTR only affects reverse lookups of the address.
explanation: Resolvers cache a record for its TTL and do not see changes until it expires. A falling TTL in an answer shows that it came from cache. Lower the TTL well before a planned address change.

question: Refer to the exhibit. The web server www.example.com is dual-stacked with the addresses 192.0.2.80 and 2001:db8:10::80. IPv4-only clients load the site normally. IPv6-only clients cannot load it by name, although the same clients can open https://[2001:db8:10::80]/ directly. What is the cause?
exhibit:
$ dig www.example.com A +noall +answer
www.example.com.    300  IN  A     192.0.2.80
$ dig www.example.com AAAA +noall +answer
www.example.com.    300  IN  AAAA  2001:db8:10::8
$ ping -6 -c 2 2001:db8:10::80
PING 2001:db8:10::80(2001:db8:10::80) 56 data bytes
64 bytes from 2001:db8:10::80: icmp_seq=1 ttl=58 time=3.12 ms
64 bytes from 2001:db8:10::80: icmp_seq=2 ttl=58 time=2.95 ms
options: The AAAA record holds the wrong address and must be corrected to 2001:db8:10::80
The A record must be changed so that it also contains the IPv6 address
A PTR record for the IPv6 address is missing from the ip6.arpa zone
The example.com zone has no NS record that IPv6 clients can use, so their queries are never answered
rationales: Correct: IPv6 clients use the AAAA record, which returns 2001:db8:10::8 instead of the address of the server. The server itself answers over IPv6, so only the record is wrong.
Wrong: an A record can hold only an IPv4 address. IPv6 addresses are published in AAAA records.
Wrong: a PTR record is used for reverse lookups, from address to name. Clients opening the site by name perform a forward lookup.
Wrong: the AAAA query in the exhibit is answered, so the zone is being found and served. The content of the answer is the fault.
explanation: A covers IPv4 and AAAA covers IPv6. If a name works over IPv4 but not IPv6, while the IPv6 address itself responds, check the AAAA record for a missing or mistyped address.

question: Refer to the exhibit. Users cannot open https://portal.example.com, but the application answers when they browse to 192.0.2.44. What is the fault?
exhibit:
$ dig portal.example.com A +noall +answer
portal.example.com.   3600  IN  CNAME  app-prod.example.com.
$ dig app-prod.example.com A +noall +answer
$ dig app-prd.example.com A +noall +answer
app-prd.example.com.  3600  IN  A      192.0.2.44
options: A CNAME record must point to an IP address, so its target should be changed to 192.0.2.44
An alias and its target cannot be in the same zone, so the CNAME is ignored
The A record for app-prd.example.com needs a matching PTR record before the alias can be followed
The CNAME points to a name that has no address record; its target should be app-prd.example.com
rationales: Wrong: the target of a CNAME is always another name, never an address.
Wrong: a CNAME may point to a name in the same zone or in a different one.
Wrong: following a CNAME is a forward lookup. PTR records are used only for reverse lookups.
Correct: the alias leads to app-prod.example.com, which returns no A record. The record that holds 192.0.2.44 is app-prd.example.com, so the CNAME target is mistyped.
explanation: A CNAME only redirects the lookup to another name. That name must itself resolve to an A or AAAA record, so always follow the chain to the end when an alias fails.

question: Refer to the exhibit. A monitoring tool lists the mail server only as 192.0.2.25 instead of showing its name. Which record must be created to fix this?
exhibit:
C:\> nslookup mail1.example.com
Server:  dns1.example.com
Address:  10.1.1.53

Name:    mail1.example.com
Address:  192.0.2.25

C:\> nslookup 192.0.2.25
Server:  dns1.example.com
Address:  10.1.1.53

*** dns1.example.com can't find 192.0.2.25: Non-existent domain
options: An A record that maps mail1.example.com to 192.0.2.25
A PTR record for 25.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa that points to mail1.example.com
A CNAME record that makes 192.0.2.25 an alias of mail1.example.com
An MX record for example.com that names mail1.example.com
rationales: Wrong: this record already exists. The first lookup returns 192.0.2.25 for the name.
Correct: the forward lookup works but the reverse lookup fails. Reverse lookups use PTR records, stored under in-addr.arpa with the octets of the address reversed.
Wrong: a CNAME makes one name an alias of another name. It is not used to map an address to a name.
Wrong: an MX record tells senders which host accepts mail for the domain. It does not provide address-to-name resolution.
explanation: Name-to-address lookups use A or AAAA records; address-to-name lookups use PTR records in in-addr.arpa (IPv4) or ip6.arpa (IPv6). One can work while the other fails.

question: A company wants 40 home-based staff to reach internal servers securely from their laptops over any Internet connection. The security team requires an IPsec tunnel from each laptop to the head-office firewall. Which solution fits this requirement?
options: A site-to-site VPN, with each laptop using the head-office firewall as its default gateway
A remote-access VPN, with VPN client software such as Cisco Secure Client on each laptop
A clientless VPN, with users opening an HTTPS session to the firewall in a web browser
A GRE tunnel from each laptop to the head-office firewall
rationales: Wrong: a site-to-site VPN joins whole networks through a VPN gateway at each site, and the hosts behind those gateways need no VPN software. A roaming laptop is not behind such a gateway.

Correct: a remote-access VPN connects an individual device to the corporate network on demand. The client software on the laptop is the tunnel endpoint and builds the IPsec tunnel to the head-office VPN gateway.
Wrong: a clientless VPN is protected by TLS in the browser, not by IPsec, and normally gives access only to web-based resources.
Wrong: GRE is an encapsulation used between routers. It provides no encryption or authentication, so it does not meet the security requirement.
explanation: Site-to-site VPNs join networks through gateways and are transparent to hosts. Remote-access VPNs join single users, normally with client software (IPsec or TLS) or, for clientless access, a browser using TLS.

question: Two branch routers form a site-to-site IPsec VPN across the Internet using ESP in tunnel mode. A host at 10.1.1.10 sends a packet to 10.2.2.20 at the other site. How is the packet carried across the Internet?
options: The original IP header with 10.1.1.10 and 10.2.2.20 stays readable at the front of the packet and only the payload behind it is encrypted
The original IP header is rewritten by NAT with the routers' public addresses and the payload is then encrypted
The whole original packet is carried in clear text behind a new IP header, with only an integrity check added
The whole original packet, including the 10.1.1.10 and 10.2.2.20 addresses, is encrypted and placed behind a new IP header that uses the routers' public addresses
rationales: Wrong: this describes transport mode, where the original IP header is kept and only the payload is protected. Private 10.x addresses in the outer header could not be routed over the Internet.
Wrong: IPsec tunnel mode does not translate the original header. It leaves the original packet intact and wraps it in a new packet.
Wrong: ESP encrypts what it carries. A new header with no encryption describes plain tunnelling such as GRE, or integrity-only protection such as AH.
Correct: tunnel mode encapsulates the complete original packet. ESP encrypts it, and a new outer IP header carries it between the two VPN gateways, so the inner addresses are hidden.
explanation: Tunnel mode protects the entire original packet and adds a new IP header (gateway to gateway), which is why it is the normal choice for site-to-site VPNs. Transport mode keeps the original IP header and protects only the payload.

question: A teleworker's IPsec VPN client sits behind a home router that performs PAT. During IKE negotiation the peers detect the address translation. How is the ESP traffic then sent so that it survives PAT?
options: It is encapsulated in UDP using port 4500
It is sent as AH (IP protocol 51) instead, because AH is not affected by address translation
It is sent as native IP protocol 50, and the home router tracks it by its TCP sequence numbers
It is encapsulated in UDP using port 500, the port used for the first IKE messages
rationales: Correct: NAT traversal (NAT-T) wraps ESP in a UDP header on port 4500. PAT can then translate the UDP port numbers as it does for any other UDP flow.
Wrong: AH is the protocol that NAT breaks. Its integrity check covers the outer IP header addresses, so a translated packet fails authentication.
Wrong: native ESP has no port numbers for PAT to translate, and the TCP header inside it is encrypted, so the home router cannot track the flow this way.
Wrong: UDP port 500 is where IKE starts. Once NAT is detected, IKE itself moves to UDP 4500 and ESP is encapsulated on port 4500 as well.
explanation: IKE begins on UDP 500. When NAT is detected, NAT-T moves IKE to UDP 4500 and encapsulates ESP (IP protocol 50) in UDP 4500 so that PAT devices can handle it.

question: Which three security services does an IPsec VPN using ESP provide for the traffic it protects? (Choose three.)
options: Confidentiality, by encrypting the payload
Guaranteed delivery, by retransmitting packets that are lost in the tunnel
Data integrity, by detecting packets that were altered in transit
Quality of service, by reserving bandwidth along the Internet path
Anti-replay protection, by rejecting duplicated or old packets using sequence numbers
Path redundancy, by load-balancing the tunnel across several service providers
rationales: Correct: ESP encrypts the protected data (for example with AES), so it cannot be read in transit.
Wrong: IPsec does not retransmit anything. Reliable delivery is left to upper-layer protocols such as TCP.
Correct: a keyed hash (HMAC) carried with each packet lets the receiver detect any modification.
Wrong: IPsec provides no bandwidth reservation. QoS is a separate function, and the Internet offers best-effort delivery only.
Correct: each packet carries a sequence number, and the receiver discards packets that fall outside its anti-replay window or repeat a number already seen.
Wrong: IPsec does not provide load balancing or redundancy. Those come from routing and tunnel design.
explanation: IPsec provides confidentiality (encryption), data integrity, origin authentication of the peer and anti-replay protection. It does not add reliability, QoS or redundancy.

question: Match each protocol used in VPN designs to its description.
pairs: Uses UDP port 500 to authenticate the peers and negotiate security associations
IP protocol 50; encrypts the protected data and can also authenticate it
IP protocol 51; provides integrity and origin authentication but no encryption
IP protocol 47; can carry multicast and routing protocol packets but gives no protection
distractors: TCP port 443; carries a browser-based clientless VPN session
explanation: IKE (UDP 500, and UDP 4500 with NAT-T) authenticates the peers and negotiates the security associations and keys. ESP (protocol 50) gives encryption plus integrity and authentication. AH (protocol 51) gives integrity and authentication only and does not work through NAT. GRE (protocol 47) is a plain tunnel that can carry multicast, so it is often combined with IPsec. TCP 443 is TLS, which is not part of the IPsec suite.

question: Two sites are joined by a classic crypto-map-based IPsec site-to-site VPN. Hosts at each site can ping each other through it, but the two VPN routers never form an OSPF adjacency across it. Which design change is the usual way to run OSPF between the sites while keeping the traffic encrypted?
options: Replace ESP with AH so that the OSPF hello packets are no longer encrypted
Change the existing IPsec VPN from tunnel mode to transport mode
Build a GRE tunnel between the routers, run OSPF on the tunnel interfaces and protect the GRE packets with IPsec
Permit UDP port 4500 between the routers so that NAT traversal carries the OSPF hellos
rationales: Wrong: encryption is not what stops the adjacency. A classic IPsec VPN carries only the unicast IP traffic selected for it, and AH would also remove confidentiality.
Wrong: changing the mode alone does not make IPsec carry multicast. Transport mode is useful here only once GRE supplies the tunnel.

Correct: GRE wraps the multicast OSPF packets in unicast GRE packets (IP protocol 47) between the routers. IPsec then encrypts those GRE packets, so routing protocols work and the traffic stays protected.
Wrong: UDP 4500 is used when a NAT device sits between the peers. It does not add multicast support to IPsec.
explanation: Classic IPsec tunnels forward unicast IP only, so multicast-based routing protocols cannot run across them. GRE over IPsec solves this: GRE carries the multicast and IPsec (often in transport mode, because GRE already adds the new IP header) encrypts the GRE packets.

question: An engineer must write a numbered IPv4 ACL that matches on the destination TCP port. Which ACL number can be used?
rationales: Wrong: 1 to 99 is the standard range. A standard ACL matches the source address only.
Wrong: 1300 to 1999 is the expanded standard range, so this ACL could still match the source address only.
Correct: extended IPv4 ACLs use 100 to 199 and the expanded range 2000 to 2699. Only an extended ACL can match protocol, destination address and ports.
Wrong: 2700 is outside the IPv4 extended range, which ends at 2699.
explanation: Standard ACLs: 1-99 and 1300-1999 (source address only). Extended ACLs: 100-199 and 2000-2699 (protocol, source, destination and ports).

question: Match each address and wildcard mask pair from an ACL entry to the range of addresses it matches.
explanation: A wildcard mask is the inverse of the subnet mask: subtract each mask octet from 255, and the result plus one is the block size. 0.0.3.255 is a /22 (third octet block of 4: 8 to 11). 0.0.7.255 is a /21 (block of 8: 8 to 15). 0.0.0.63 is a /26 (64 addresses). 0.0.0.31 is a /27 (32 addresses: 64 to 95). 0.0.0.3 is a /30 (4 addresses: 8 to 11). The unused range 10.4.8.0 to 10.4.9.255 would need 0.0.1.255.

question: R1 applies the ACL WEB-FILTER inbound on its LAN interface. A host at 10.20.5.77 opens an HTTPS session to the server at 192.0.2.10. What happens to the first packet of the session?
exhibit:
R1# show access-lists WEB-FILTER
Extended IP access list WEB-FILTER
    10 deny tcp 10.20.4.0 0.0.1.255 host 192.0.2.10 eq www (8 matches)
    20 permit tcp 10.20.0.0 0.0.3.255 any eq 443 (1362 matches)
    30 deny ip 10.20.0.0 0.0.255.255 host 192.0.2.10 (41 matches)
    40 permit ip any any (5270 matches)
options: It is denied by entry 10
It is permitted by entry 20
It is denied by entry 30
It is permitted by entry 40
rationales: Wrong: the source (10.20.4.0 to 10.20.5.255) and destination of entry 10 match, but the entry matches destination port 80 (www). HTTPS uses TCP port 443.
Wrong: 10.20.0.0 with wildcard 0.0.3.255 covers 10.20.0.0 to 10.20.3.255 only, so 10.20.5.77 is not matched by entry 20.
Correct: entries 10 and 20 do not match, and entry 30 is the first that does: the source is inside 10.20.0.0/16 and the destination is host 192.0.2.10, for any IP protocol.
Wrong: processing stops at the first matching entry, which is entry 30. Entry 40 is never evaluated for this packet.
explanation: ACLs are processed top down and stop at the first match. Check every field of each entry (protocol, source range from the wildcard mask, destination, port) before moving to the next one.

question: GigabitEthernet0/0/1 on R2 is the default gateway for the LAN 10.1.1.0/24. The aim was to stop only host 10.1.1.50 from leaving the LAN, but since these commands were entered no host on the LAN can reach other networks. Which command fixes this while still blocking 10.1.1.50?
exhibit:
R2(config)# access-list 10 deny host 10.1.1.50
R2(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1
R2(config-if)# ip access-group 10 in
R2(config-if)# end
R2#
options: access-list 10 permit host 10.1.1.50
access-list 11 permit any
ip access-group 10 out, entered on GigabitEthernet0/0/1
access-list 10 permit any
rationales: Wrong: this appends a permit for the blocked host after the deny, so it is never matched, and every other host still falls through to the implicit deny.
Wrong: this creates a separate ACL 11 that is not applied to any interface. ACL 10 is unchanged.
Wrong: this adds the same ACL in the outbound direction as well. The inbound ACL still drops the LAN hosts' traffic.
Correct: the entry is appended after the deny. Host 10.1.1.50 still matches the deny first, and all other sources now match the permit instead of the implicit deny.
explanation: Every ACL ends with an invisible 'deny any'. An ACL that contains only deny entries therefore blocks everything, so add an explicit permit for the traffic that must still pass.

question: An engineer must allow remote CLI sessions to R1 only from the management subnet 10.99.0.0/24, using a named standard ACL. The ACL is completed before it is applied. Put the commands in the order in which they are entered, starting from privileged EXEC mode.
explanation: The named ACL is created in global configuration mode and its entry is added in ACL configuration mode. It is then applied to the vty lines with 'access-class ... in', which filters incoming Telnet and SSH sessions to the router by source address. 'ip access-group' is the interface command and is not used on lines.

question: BRANCH-IN is applied inbound on the LAN interface that serves 10.5.0.0/24. Users report that names no longer resolve. The hosts send their DNS queries over UDP to the server 198.51.100.53. Which commands fix the problem?
exhibit:
R1# show access-lists BRANCH-IN
Extended IP access list BRANCH-IN
    10 permit tcp 10.5.0.0 0.0.0.255 any eq www (731 matches)
    20 permit tcp 10.5.0.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 443 (9204 matches)
    30 deny ip any any log (388 matches)
options: ip access-list extended BRANCH-IN, then: permit udp 10.5.0.0 0.0.0.255 host 198.51.100.53 eq 53
ip access-list extended BRANCH-IN, then: 25 permit udp 10.5.0.0 0.0.0.255 host 198.51.100.53 eq 53
access-list BRANCH-IN permit udp 10.5.0.0 0.0.0.255 host 198.51.100.53 eq 53
ip access-list extended BRANCH-IN, then: 35 permit udp 10.5.0.0 0.0.0.255 host 198.51.100.53 eq 53
ip access-list extended BRANCH-IN, then: 25 permit udp host 198.51.100.53 10.5.0.0 0.0.0.255 eq 53
rationales: Wrong: without a sequence number the entry is added at the end as entry 40, after the 'deny ip any any' at 30, so it is never reached.
Correct: sequence number 25 places the permit before the deny at 30, and the entry matches UDP from the LAN to the DNS server on destination port 53.
Wrong: the global 'access-list' command accepts ACL numbers only. A named ACL is edited with 'ip access-list extended NAME'.
Wrong: sequence number 35 puts the entry after the 'deny ip any any' at 30, which already matches and drops the DNS queries.
Wrong: source and destination are reversed. Inbound on the LAN interface the queries come from 10.5.0.0/24 and go to 198.51.100.53.
explanation: Named (and numbered) ACLs can be edited in ACL configuration mode by sequence number. A new entry must have a sequence number lower than any entry that would otherwise match the traffic first.

question: Users on the LAN 192.168.10.0/24 should be able to use only HTTP, HTTPS and DNS through R1. After this configuration is applied, no user can browse at all. What is wrong?
exhibit:
R1# show access-lists LAN-WEB
Extended IP access list LAN-WEB
    10 permit tcp 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255 any eq www
    20 permit tcp 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255 any eq 443
    30 permit udp 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255 any eq domain
R1# show running-config interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0
Building configuration...

Current configuration : 139 bytes
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/0
 description LAN 192.168.10.0/24
 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
 ip access-group LAN-WEB out
end
options: The ACL is applied in the wrong direction; it should be applied inbound on GigabitEthernet0/0/0
The wildcard mask is wrong; it should be 255.255.255.0
The eq keyword is in the wrong place; it must follow the source network because the clients use these ports as source ports
A named ACL cannot be applied with ip access-group; it must be applied with access-class
rationales: Correct: outbound on the LAN interface the ACL sees packets going to the users, whose source is a remote server and not 192.168.10.0/24. Nothing matches, so the implicit deny drops every reply. Applied inbound, the ACL sees the users' requests, which the entries were written for.
Wrong: 0.0.0.255 is the correct wildcard mask for a /24. 255.255.255.0 is the subnet mask; used as a wildcard it would ignore the first three octets.
Wrong: clients use random high source ports. The well-known ports 80, 443 and 53 are the destination ports of their requests, so eq belongs after the destination.
Wrong: named ACLs are applied to interfaces with ip access-group in the same way as numbered ACLs. access-class is used on vty lines.
explanation: Read each entry from the point of view of the packet in the direction the ACL is applied. An ACL written with the LAN as source must be applied inbound on the LAN interface (or outbound on the exit interface).

question: A PC on R1's LAN cannot ping 203.0.113.2, the ISP router directly connected to GigabitEthernet0/0/1. The same ping from the R1 CLI succeeds. What explains the difference?
exhibit:
R1# show access-lists 120
Extended IP access list 120
    10 deny icmp any any (15 matches)
    20 permit ip any any (2210 matches)
R1# show running-config interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1
Building configuration...

Current configuration : 105 bytes
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1
 ip address 203.0.113.1 255.255.255.252
 ip access-group 120 out
end
R1# ping 203.0.113.2
Type escape sequence to abort.
Sending 5, 100-byte ICMP Echos to 203.0.113.2, timeout is 2 seconds:
!!!!!
Success rate is 100 percent (5/5), round-trip min/avg/max = 1/1/2 ms
options: ICMP packets generated by IOS are classified as IP rather than ICMP, so R1's pings match entry 20
An outbound ACL does not filter packets that the router itself originates
The PC's pings are dropped by the implicit deny, which applies only to transit traffic
Entry 10 matches only ICMP echo replies, and R1 receives replies rather than sending them
rationales: Wrong: an echo request from the router is ordinary ICMP. It is not matched against the outbound ACL at all, so it does not hit entry 20 either.

Correct: interface ACLs applied outbound filter transit traffic only. Packets created by the router itself, such as its own pings, bypass the outbound ACL, while the PC's echo requests are transit traffic and match entry 10.
Wrong: the PC's echo requests are dropped by the explicit 'deny icmp any any' at entry 10 (note its match counter), not by the implicit deny.
Wrong: 'deny icmp any any' matches every ICMP type, including echo requests. The replies to R1 arrive inbound, where no ACL is applied.
explanation: Outbound ACLs are not applied to traffic the router generates itself. Never use a ping from the router to prove that an outbound ACL permits something; test with transit traffic.

question: ACL 102 already exists on R1. An engineer now enters ip access-group 102 in on GigabitEthernet0/0/1. What is the result?
exhibit:
R1# show ip interface GigabitEthernet0/0/1
GigabitEthernet0/0/1 is up, line protocol is up
  Internet address is 10.10.20.1/24
  Broadcast address is 255.255.255.255
  Address determined by non-volatile memory
  MTU is 1500 bytes
  Helper address is not set
  Directed broadcast forwarding is disabled
  Outgoing Common access list is not set
  Outgoing access list is not set
  Inbound Common access list is not set
  Inbound  access list is 101
  Proxy ARP is enabled
<output omitted>
options: Inbound packets are checked against ACL 101 first and then against ACL 102
The command is rejected until no ip access-group 101 in is entered
The entries of ACL 102 are appended to the end of ACL 101
ACL 102 replaces ACL 101 as the inbound IPv4 ACL on the interface
rationales: Wrong: an interface never chains two IPv4 ACLs in the same direction. Only one can be active.
Wrong: IOS accepts the command without complaint and simply overwrites the previous inbound ACL reference.
Wrong: applying an ACL to an interface never changes the contents of any ACL. ACL 101 still exists unchanged; it is just no longer applied here.
Correct: an interface can have only one ACL per protocol per direction. The new ip access-group command replaces the existing inbound ACL 101 with ACL 102.
explanation: One ACL per interface, per direction (in and out), per protocol (IPv4, IPv6). Entering a second 'ip access-group ... in' silently replaces the first, which can remove filtering that was relied on.

question: An entry in an extended ACL must permit SSH from the single host 10.8.8.8 to every device in 10.50.0.0/16, and nothing else. Which two entries do exactly this? (Choose two.)
rationales: Correct: 'host 10.8.8.8' matches that one source, 0.0.255.255 is the wildcard for a /16, and 'eq 22' after the destination matches SSH as the destination port.
Wrong: 'eq 22' placed after the source matches the source port. An SSH client uses a random high source port, and port 22 is the destination.
Correct: an address with wildcard 0.0.0.0 means every bit must match, which is the same as the host keyword. The rest of the entry is identical to the first correct one.
Wrong: wildcard 255.255.255.255 ignores every bit of the address, so this is the same as 'any' and permits SSH from all sources.
Wrong: port operators such as eq are only valid with tcp or udp. With the ip keyword the command is rejected.
Wrong: 255.255.0.0 is the subnet mask, not the wildcard. As a wildcard it ignores the first two octets and requires the last two to be 0.0, so it does not match the hosts in 10.50.0.0/16.
explanation: 'host A' equals 'A 0.0.0.0' and 'any' equals '0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255'. In an extended entry the order is protocol, source [source port], destination [destination port], and port matches need tcp or udp.

question: R1's GigabitEthernet0/0/1 connects to a partner network, and the ACL PARTNER-IN is applied inbound on it. Hosts on the internal LAN 10.10.0.0/16 must be able to open TCP sessions to partner servers and receive the replies, but partner hosts must not be able to open new TCP sessions to the internal LAN. No NAT is used. Which entry in PARTNER-IN achieves this?
options: permit tcp any 10.10.0.0 0.0.255.255 established
permit ip any 10.10.0.0 0.0.255.255 established
permit tcp 10.10.0.0 0.0.255.255 any established
rationales: Wrong: this permits new sessions from the partner to port 443 on internal hosts. Replies to internal clients are addressed to their random high ports, so they would not match it.

Correct: established matches only TCP segments that have the ACK or RST bit set, which is true of replies but not of the initial SYN of a new session. Return traffic is permitted and new inbound sessions fall through to the implicit deny.
Wrong: established is an option of the tcp protocol keyword only. IOS rejects it with ip.
Wrong: source and destination are reversed. Packets arriving inbound on GigabitEthernet0/0/1 have partner addresses as source and 10.10.0.0/16 as destination.
explanation: The established keyword (TCP only) matches segments with ACK or RST set, so it lets replies to internally initiated sessions back in while the first SYN of an externally initiated session is not matched.

question: Hosts in 10.1.10.0/24 must be stopped from reaching the web server 10.3.30.80 on TCP port 443. All of their other traffic, and all traffic from other hosts, must be unaffected. Which two choices follow Cisco's ACL design guidance? (Choose two.)
options: Use a standard ACL, because it can match the destination host address
Use an extended ACL, because the entry must match the destination address and TCP port
Apply the ACL as close as possible to the server, because that is the guidance for extended ACLs
Apply the ACL inbound on the router interface closest to 10.1.10.0/24, so that unwanted packets are dropped before they cross the network
Number the ACL in the 1300-1999 range, which is reserved for extended ACLs
rationales: Wrong: a standard ACL matches only the source address. It could not single out the server or port 443, so it would block all traffic from 10.1.10.0/24 wherever it was applied.
Correct: only an extended ACL can match protocol, source, destination and port in one entry.
Wrong: 'close to the destination' is the guidance for standard ACLs, which cannot match a destination. Extended ACLs are placed close to the source.
Correct: because an extended ACL identifies the traffic precisely, it is placed as close to the source as possible, which avoids carrying packets across the network only to drop them.
Wrong: 1300-1999 is the expanded standard range. Extended ACLs use 100-199 and 2000-2699.
explanation: Extended ACLs go close to the source because they can be specific. Standard ACLs go close to the destination because they match the source only and would otherwise block too much.

question: An engineer tries to enable port security on a new access switch and sees the message in the exhibit. Which interface command must be entered first?
exhibit:
SW1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet1/0/5
SW1(config-if)# switchport port-security
Command rejected: GigabitEthernet1/0/5 is a dynamic port.
SW1(config-if)#
options: switchport access vlan 10
switchport port-security maximum 1
switchport mode access
spanning-tree portfast
rationales: Wrong: this assigns the access VLAN, but the port still negotiates its mode with DTP and so remains a dynamic port.
Wrong: this sets a port security parameter (and 1 is already the default). It does not change the port from dynamic to static, so the feature still cannot be enabled.
Correct: port security can be enabled only on a static access or static trunk port. Setting the mode to access removes the dynamic (DTP-negotiated) state, after which the command is accepted.
Wrong: PortFast affects spanning-tree convergence on the port. It has no bearing on whether port security can be enabled.
explanation: Port security is not supported on ports in a dynamic (auto or desirable) mode. Configure 'switchport mode access' (or 'switchport mode trunk') before 'switchport port-security'.

question: The PC on GigabitEthernet1/0/7 was replaced by a new laptop this morning and the port stopped working. Errdisable recovery is not configured. Which action restores service for the new laptop while keeping port security in place?
exhibit:
SW1# show port-security interface GigabitEthernet1/0/7
Port Security              : Enabled
Port Status                : Secure-shutdown
Violation Mode             : Shutdown
Aging Time                 : 0 mins
Aging Type                 : Absolute
SecureStatic Address Aging : Disabled
Maximum MAC Addresses      : 1
Total MAC Addresses        : 1
Configured MAC Addresses   : 0
Sticky MAC Addresses       : 1
Last Source Address:Vlan   : 0050.56ab.12cd:10
Security Violation Count   : 1
options: Enter shutdown and then no shutdown on the interface; no other change is needed
Enter switchport port-security violation restrict on the interface; no other change is needed
Wait for the secure MAC address to age out, after which the port recovers by itself
Remove the old PC's sticky secure MAC address from the port, then enter shutdown and no shutdown on the interface
rationales: Wrong: this re-enables the port, but the old PC's sticky address still fills the single allowed slot. The laptop's first frame causes another violation and the port is err-disabled again.
Wrong: changing the violation mode does not bring a port out of err-disabled, and with the old sticky address still present the laptop's frames would still be dropped.
Wrong: the aging time is 0, which means secure addresses never age out, and an err-disabled port does not recover by itself unless errdisable recovery is configured.

Correct: the output shows one sticky address (the old PC), a maximum of one, and a violation from another source address, which left the port in Secure-shutdown (err-disabled). The stale sticky entry must be cleared so the laptop's MAC can be learned, and the port must be bounced to leave the err-disabled state.
explanation: Secure-shutdown means the port is err-disabled by a port security violation. Fix the cause first (here a stale sticky MAC address, removable with 'clear port-security sticky interface ...' or by deleting the sticky line), then recover with shutdown / no shutdown or with errdisable recovery.

question: Match each port security keyword to its effect.
pairs: Drops frames from unknown source MAC addresses silently: no log message and no violation counter increment
Drops frames from unknown source MAC addresses, increments the violation counter and logs the event; the port stays up
Puts the port into the err-disabled state, increments the violation counter and logs the event
Adds dynamically learned MAC addresses to the running configuration as secure addresses
distractors: Forwards frames from unknown source MAC addresses but logs each one
explanation: The three violation modes differ in what happens beyond dropping the offending frames: protect does nothing more, restrict also counts and logs, and shutdown (the default) err-disables the port as well as counting and logging. Sticky is not a violation mode: it turns learned addresses into secure addresses in the running configuration. No mode forwards the offending frames.

question: An engineer enters only switchport mode access and switchport port-security on an interface. Which two settings are now in effect on the port? (Choose two.)
options: A maximum of one secure MAC address
A maximum of two secure MAC addresses, to allow for an IP phone and a PC
Violation mode restrict
Violation mode shutdown
Sticky learning of the first source MAC address
rationales: Correct: the default maximum is one secure MAC address per port.
Wrong: the default is one. A higher limit for a phone plus a PC must be set with switchport port-security maximum.
Wrong: restrict keeps the port up while dropping and logging, but it must be configured explicitly. It is not the default.
Correct: the default violation mode is shutdown, which err-disables the port when a violation occurs.
Wrong: by default the address is learned dynamically and is not added to the configuration. Sticky learning needs switchport port-security mac-address sticky.
explanation: Port security defaults: maximum 1 secure MAC address, violation mode shutdown, dynamic (non-sticky) learning with no aging.

question: The DHCP server for VLAN 20 is reached through DSW1. Since the configuration in the exhibit was applied to access switch SW2, PCs in VLAN 20 no longer receive addresses. Which command solves the problem while keeping the protection against rogue DHCP servers on access ports?
exhibit:
SW2# show running-config
<output omitted>
ip dhcp snooping vlan 20
no ip dhcp snooping information option
ip dhcp snooping
!
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/1
 description Staff PC
 switchport access vlan 20
 switchport mode access
 ip dhcp snooping limit rate 15
!
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/24
 description Uplink to DSW1
 switchport mode trunk
<output omitted>
options: ip dhcp snooping trust on GigabitEthernet1/0/24
ip dhcp snooping trust on GigabitEthernet1/0/1
ip dhcp snooping limit rate 100 on GigabitEthernet1/0/1
no ip dhcp snooping vlan 20 in global configuration mode
rationales: Correct: all ports are untrusted by default, so the server's DHCPOFFER and DHCPACK messages arriving on the uplink are dropped. The port that leads to the legitimate server must be trusted.
Wrong: this trusts the PC's port, which would let a rogue server connected there answer clients, and the genuine replies arriving on the uplink would still be dropped.
Wrong: the limit of 15 DHCP packets per second is not the fault. A single PC does not exceed it, and exceeding it would err-disable the port rather than silently block leases.
Wrong: this would restore DHCP, but only by switching DHCP snooping off for the VLAN, which removes the protection.
explanation: With DHCP snooping, server messages (OFFER, ACK, NAK) are accepted only on trusted ports. Trust the uplinks and server-facing ports with 'ip dhcp snooping trust' and leave host ports untrusted.

question: Which two statements about DHCP snooping are true? (Choose two.)
options: DHCPDISCOVER messages that arrive on an untrusted port are dropped
Every port in a snooped VLAN is untrusted until ip dhcp snooping trust is configured on it
Trunk ports are trusted by default and access ports are untrusted by default
DHCPOFFER and DHCPACK messages that arrive on an untrusted port are dropped
The binding table records the hosts that are connected to trusted ports
rationales: Wrong: DISCOVER is a client message. Clients live on untrusted ports, so their messages are accepted there and forwarded towards the trusted ports.
Correct: untrusted is the default state for every port. Trust is always configured explicitly, per interface.
Wrong: the default does not depend on the port mode. Trunks and access ports alike are untrusted until configured otherwise.
Correct: OFFER and ACK are sent only by servers. On an untrusted port they indicate a rogue DHCP server, so the switch discards them.
Wrong: the binding table records the clients learned on untrusted ports (MAC address, IP address, lease time, VLAN and interface). Devices behind trusted ports are not listed.
explanation: DHCP snooping: all ports are untrusted by default; server-type messages are dropped on untrusted ports; client leases seen on untrusted ports are recorded in the binding table.

question: DHCP snooping is active on an access switch. A new client connects to an untrusted access port and the DHCP server is reached through the trusted uplink. Put the events in the order in which they occur.
items: The client broadcasts a DHCPDISCOVER, which the switch accepts on the untrusted port
The server's DHCPOFFER arrives on the trusted uplink and is forwarded to the client
The client broadcasts a DHCPREQUEST for the offered address
The server's DHCPACK arrives on the trusted uplink
The switch records the client's MAC address, IP address, VLAN, port and lease time in the binding table
explanation: The normal Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge exchange takes place, with client messages allowed in on the untrusted port and server messages allowed in only on the trusted uplink. The switch creates the binding entry when it sees the DHCPACK, because only then is the lease confirmed. Dynamic ARP Inspection later relies on that entry.

question: An engineer entered ip dhcp snooping vlan 30 on SW3 and trusted the uplink. A rogue DHCP server on an access port in VLAN 30 is still handing out addresses. Based on the exhibit, which command is missing?
exhibit:
SW3# show ip dhcp snooping
Switch DHCP snooping is disabled
DHCP snooping is configured on following VLANs:
30
DHCP snooping is operational on following VLANs:
none
<output omitted>
options: ip dhcp snooping vlan 30, entered on each access interface
no ip dhcp snooping trust, entered on each access interface
ip dhcp snooping, entered in global configuration mode
ip arp inspection vlan 30, entered in global configuration mode
rationales: Wrong: the VLAN list is a global setting and is already present, as the 'configured on following VLANs' line shows. It is not an interface command.
Wrong: access ports are untrusted by default, so there is no trust setting to remove.

Correct: the first line shows that snooping is disabled globally, so it is configured for VLAN 30 but operational on none. The feature needs both the global ip dhcp snooping command and the VLAN list.
Wrong: this enables Dynamic ARP Inspection, which validates ARP packets. It does not filter DHCP server messages.
explanation: DHCP snooping needs two global commands: 'ip dhcp snooping' to switch the feature on and 'ip dhcp snooping vlan <list>' to say where. Compare the 'configured' and 'operational' VLAN lines to spot a missing one.

question: DHCP snooping and ip arp inspection vlan 20 are enabled on SW2. DHCP clients in VLAN 20 work normally, but a printer on GigabitEthernet1/0/9 with the static address 10.20.0.50 has lost all connectivity. The port must stay untrusted. Which action restores the printer's connectivity?
options: Configure ip dhcp snooping trust on GigabitEthernet1/0/9
Create an ARP ACL that permits the printer's IP and MAC address pair and apply it to VLAN 20 with ip arp inspection filter
Configure the printer's MAC address with switchport port-security mac-address on GigabitEthernet1/0/9
Configure ip arp inspection limit rate 100 on GigabitEthernet1/0/9
rationales: Wrong: DHCP snooping trust decides where DHCP server messages are accepted. It does not change how DAI validates ARP packets on the port.

Correct: DAI checks ARP packets on untrusted ports against the DHCP snooping binding table. A statically addressed host never obtains a lease, so it has no binding and its ARP packets are dropped. An ARP ACL supplies the permitted IP-to-MAC mapping for such hosts.
Wrong: port security controls which source MAC addresses may use the port. DAI does not consult the port security table.
Wrong: the ARP packets are dropped because no binding matches them, not because the printer exceeds the ARP rate limit.
explanation: DAI validates the sender IP and MAC in ARP packets on untrusted ports against DHCP snooping bindings. Hosts with static addresses need an ARP ACL ('arp access-list', applied with 'ip arp inspection filter NAME vlan X') or a trusted port.

question: SW2 is an access switch. The default gateway for VLAN 20 is a statically addressed SVI on DSW1, reached through Gi1/0/24. DHCP snooping works and the PCs obtain leases. Immediately after ip arp inspection vlan 20 was entered on SW2, the PCs could no longer reach their default gateway. Which command fixes this while still inspecting ARP from the PCs?
exhibit:
SW2# show ip arp inspection interfaces

 Interface        Trust State     Rate (pps)    Burst Interval
 ---------------  -----------     ----------    --------------
 Gi1/0/1          Untrusted               15                 1
 Gi1/0/2          Untrusted               15                 1
 Gi1/0/24         Untrusted               15                 1
options: ip dhcp snooping trust on Gi1/0/24
ip arp inspection limit rate none on Gi1/0/24
ip arp inspection trust on Gi1/0/1 and Gi1/0/2
ip arp inspection trust on Gi1/0/24
rationales: Wrong: the PCs obtain leases, so the uplink is already trusted for DHCP snooping. DAI keeps its own, separate trust setting.
Wrong: this removes the ARP rate limit on the uplink, but the gateway's ARP packets would still fail validation on an untrusted port.
Wrong: this stops inspection of the PCs' ARP packets, which removes the protection, and the gateway's ARP packets arriving on the uplink would still be dropped.

Correct: the exhibit shows the uplink as untrusted. The gateway's address is static, so SW2 has no DHCP snooping binding for it and drops its ARP replies arriving on Gi1/0/24. Trusting the uplink for DAI lets ARP from the distribution layer through uninspected.
explanation: DAI trust is configured separately from DHCP snooping trust. Trust the uplinks to other switches and routers with 'ip arp inspection trust' and leave host ports untrusted so their ARP packets are inspected.

question: An attacker on VLAN 20 sends forged ARP replies that map the default gateway's IP address to the attacker's own MAC address. Which switch feature is designed to drop these replies, and what does it normally check them against?
options: DHCP snooping, using its list of trusted ports
Port security, using the secure MAC address table
Dynamic ARP Inspection, using the DHCP snooping binding table
Storm control, using the broadcast threshold
rationales: Wrong: DHCP snooping filters DHCP messages, not ARP. It supplies the binding table but does not inspect ARP packets itself.
Wrong: the attacker sends the frames from its own genuine MAC address, so port security sees no violation. Port security does not look inside ARP packets.

Correct: DAI intercepts ARP packets on untrusted ports and compares the sender IP and MAC with the DHCP snooping bindings. The gateway's IP paired with the attacker's MAC matches no binding, so the packet is dropped.
Wrong: storm control limits the volume of broadcast, multicast or unicast traffic. A few forged ARP replies are well below any threshold and are not examined for content.
explanation: ARP spoofing (ARP poisoning) is stopped by Dynamic ARP Inspection, which depends on the DHCP snooping binding table to know the legitimate IP-to-MAC pairs.

question: A faulty NIC on the device attached to this port starts sending broadcasts that reach 12 per cent of the interface bandwidth. What does the switch do?
exhibit:
SW1# show running-config interface GigabitEthernet1/0/10
Building configuration...

Current configuration : 121 bytes
!
interface GigabitEthernet1/0/10
 switchport access vlan 30
 switchport mode access
 storm-control broadcast level 5.00
end
options: It places the port in the err-disabled state
It keeps forwarding the frames and only sends an SNMP trap
It drops all traffic on the port, including unicast, until the storm ends
It drops broadcast frames on the port until the level falls below the threshold; the port stays up
rationales: Wrong: the port is err-disabled only if storm-control action shutdown is configured, and it is not in this configuration.
Wrong: with no action configured the switch filters the traffic. A trap is sent only if storm-control action trap is configured.
Wrong: the threshold is configured for broadcast traffic only, so storm control does not act on unicast traffic on this port.

Correct: the broadcast level is above the 5 per cent threshold and no action is configured, so the default applies: the broadcast traffic is suppressed until it drops back below the threshold, and the port remains up.
explanation: Storm control thresholds are set per traffic type (broadcast, multicast, unicast). The default action is to drop the offending traffic type; 'storm-control action shutdown' err-disables the port and 'storm-control action trap' sends an SNMP trap.

question: An access port must be err-disabled automatically if broadcast traffic exceeds 10 per cent of the interface bandwidth. Which two interface commands are required? (Choose two.)
options: storm-control broadcast level pps 10
storm-control broadcast level 10
storm-control action trap
storm-control action shutdown
switchport port-security violation shutdown
storm-control unicast level 10
rationales: Wrong: with the pps keyword the threshold is 10 packets per second, not 10 per cent of the bandwidth.
Correct: without a unit keyword the level is a percentage of the interface bandwidth, so this sets the broadcast threshold to 10 per cent.
Wrong: this action sends an SNMP trap when a storm is detected. It does not err-disable the port.
Correct: this changes the action taken when the threshold is exceeded from the default (dropping the traffic) to err-disabling the port.
Wrong: this is the port security violation mode. It reacts to unauthorised source MAC addresses, not to traffic volume.
Wrong: this sets a threshold for unicast traffic. The requirement is about broadcast traffic.
explanation: 'storm-control {broadcast | multicast | unicast} level <percent>' sets the threshold and 'storm-control action {shutdown | trap}' changes what happens when it is exceeded. With no action configured, the excess traffic type is simply dropped.

question: A user connects a home router to an access port in VLAN 10. It starts sending IPv6 Router Advertisements, and nearby hosts begin to use it as their IPv6 default gateway. The legitimate router is reached through the switch's uplink. Which measure stops this?
options: Enable DHCP snooping on VLAN 10
Apply IPv6 RA guard to the host-facing access ports, so that Router Advertisements received on them are dropped
Enable Dynamic ARP Inspection on VLAN 10
Apply IPv6 RA guard with the host role to the uplink that leads to the legitimate router
rationales: Wrong: DHCP snooping filters IPv4 DHCP server messages. Router Advertisements are ICMPv6 Neighbor Discovery messages and are not affected by it.
Correct: RA guard is an IPv6 first-hop security feature. On ports where only hosts should be connected, it drops incoming Router Advertisements, so a rogue device cannot present itself as a router.
Wrong: DAI validates IPv4 ARP packets. IPv6 does not use ARP; it uses Neighbor Discovery.

Wrong: this would drop the legitimate router's advertisements arriving on the uplink, leaving the hosts with no valid IPv6 gateway, while the rogue advertisements on the access port would still be accepted.
explanation: RA guard blocks rogue IPv6 Router Advertisements. It is applied to host-facing ports (for example with 'ipv6 nd raguard attach-policy' and a policy whose device role is host); the port towards the real router is left to accept RAs.

question: A NOC is comparing two AI tools. Tool A answers engineers' questions with text based on the prompt it is given. Tool B is given the goal "find out why branch 12 cannot reach the data centre"; it then decides which devices to query, runs show commands through their APIs, reads the results and chooses its next step until it can report a root cause. Which characteristic makes Tool B agentic AI?
options: It was trained on a larger set of vendor documentation than Tool A.
It works towards a goal over several steps by planning, calling tools and acting on what it observes.
It generates human-readable text in response to a prompt.
It forecasts future faults from historical telemetry by using a trained statistical model.
rationales: Wrong: The amount of training data affects what a model knows, not whether it can plan and act. A chatbot with a huge training set is still not agentic.
Correct: Pursuing a goal across multiple steps, choosing and calling tools, then adjusting to the results is what makes AI agentic.
Wrong: This describes generative AI in general and applies equally to Tool A, so it does not distinguish the agentic tool.
Wrong: Forecasting from historical data is predictive AI (traditional machine learning). Tool B is investigating and acting, not forecasting.
explanation: Agentic AI is defined by autonomy towards a goal: it plans, uses tools or APIs, observes the results and iterates. A generative chatbot only produces content from a prompt, and predictive AI only forecasts from historical data.

question: An agentic AI assistant is asked to resolve a ticket that reports slow access to an application. A human-in-the-loop guardrail is in place for changes. Put the stages of the assistant's workflow in the order in which they normally occur.
items: Receive the goal from the engineer or the ticket
Plan which devices and data need to be checked
Call tools or APIs to collect show output and telemetry
Analyse the collected data and identify a probable root cause
Propose a remediation and wait for an engineer to approve it
Apply the approved change and verify that the fault has cleared
explanation: An agent starts from a goal, plans, uses tools to gather evidence and reasons over the results before it proposes anything. With a human-in-the-loop guardrail the change is applied only after an engineer approves it, and the agent then verifies the outcome.

question: An engineer asks an AI network assistant why users behind R1 interface GigabitEthernet0/1 have lost connectivity. The assistant's reply and the real device output are shown. How should the engineer evaluate the recommendation?
exhibit:
Assistant: GigabitEthernet0/1 has been shut down by an administrator.
Enter interface configuration mode and issue "no shutdown" to
restore service.

R1# show ip interface brief
Interface           IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
GigabitEthernet0/0  203.0.113.1     YES NVRAM  up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/1  192.0.2.1       YES NVRAM  down                  down
GigabitEthernet0/2  unassigned      YES NVRAM  administratively down down
options: It is correct. A Status of down shows that the shutdown command is configured on the interface.
It is incomplete. The no shutdown command takes effect only after the configuration is saved with copy running-config startup-config.
It is wrong. The interface is enabled but has no link, so the cabling or the far-end port should be checked; no shutdown would change nothing.
It is wrong. The interface is down because its IP address was loaded from NVRAM and is no longer valid.
rationales: Wrong: An interface that has been shut down is reported as "administratively down", as GigabitEthernet0/2 is. GigabitEthernet0/1 shows only "down".
Wrong: IOS configuration commands take effect immediately in the running configuration. Saving only preserves them across a reload, and the diagnosis is wrong in any case.
Correct: Status down with protocol down, without the word "administratively", means the interface is not shut down but detects no signal: a Layer 1 problem.
Wrong: Method NVRAM simply means the address came from the startup configuration, and the OK? column shows YES. It has nothing to do with the interface state.
explanation: Always check an AI recommendation against real device output. A status of "administratively down" means the shutdown command is present; plain "down/down" means the interface is enabled but has no link, which is a physical-layer fault.

question: An engineer asks an AI assistant how to allow VLAN 30 on the existing trunk between SW1 and SW2. The assistant's recommendation and the current state of the trunk are shown. What is the best evaluation of the recommendation?
exhibit:
Assistant: To allow VLAN 30 on the trunk, apply:
  interface GigabitEthernet1/0/24
   switchport trunk allowed vlan 30

SW1# show interfaces trunk

Port        Mode             Encapsulation  Status        Native vlan
Gi1/0/24    on               802.1q         trunking      1

Port        Vlans allowed on trunk
Gi1/0/24    10,20

Port        Vlans allowed and active in management domain
Gi1/0/24    10,20

Port        Vlans in spanning tree forwarding state and not pruned
Gi1/0/24    10,20
options: It would cause an outage: the command replaces the allowed list with VLAN 30 alone, so the add keyword is needed to keep VLANs 10 and 20.
It is correct and safe: the command appends VLAN 30 to the existing allowed list.
It is wrong: VLAN 30 must be made the native VLAN before it can be allowed on the trunk.
It is incomplete: the trunk must first be set to dynamic desirable mode before the allowed list can be changed.
rationales: Correct: Without the add keyword the command overwrites the allowed list. VLANs 10 and 20 would be removed from the trunk and their traffic would stop.
Wrong: Appending needs "switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30". The command as written sets the list to VLAN 30 only.
Wrong: The native VLAN is the VLAN carried untagged; a VLAN does not need to be native to be allowed. Changing it would also create a native VLAN mismatch.
Wrong: The allowed list can be edited on a trunk in any mode, including the static "on" mode shown. The DTP mode is unrelated to the allowed list.
explanation: A recommendation can be syntactically valid and still be harmful. "switchport trunk allowed vlan 30" overwrites the list; "switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30" appends to it. This is why AI-generated changes are verified against device state and approved by a human first.

question: A company plans to let an agentic AI assistant carry out remediation on production switches. Which two guardrails should be put in place? (Choose two.)
options: Require an engineer to approve each proposed configuration change before the agent applies it.
Let the agent use a shared privilege 15 account so that it is never blocked during an incident.
Give the agent its own account, limited to the commands its tasks need, with every action logged.
Accept the commands the agent generates without review, because they are derived from vendor documentation.
Turn off command accounting for the agent's sessions to reduce the load on the AAA server.
rationales: Correct: Human-in-the-loop approval stops a mistaken or hallucinated change from reaching production unchecked.
Wrong: A shared, fully privileged account breaks least privilege and makes it impossible to tell the agent's actions from an engineer's.
Correct: A dedicated least-privilege identity limits the damage a wrong action can do, and logging provides an audit trail of what the agent did.
Wrong: Generative models can produce plausible but invalid or harmful commands. Output must be checked against the real device and its current state.
Wrong: Removing accounting removes the audit trail, which is one of the main controls needed for an autonomous system that changes the network.
explanation: Agentic AI can act, so it needs the same controls as any other operator: human approval for changes, least-privilege access and a full audit trail. Its output can include invented (hallucinated) or unsuitable commands, so it must be verified, not trusted blindly.

question: Match each prompt component to the sentence that supplies it in a prompt sent to a generative AI system.
pairs: "You are a senior network engineer who mentors junior staff."
"Compare the two interface configurations below and list every difference."
"Present the answer as a table with the columns Setting, R1 and R2."
"The excerpt contains no passwords or customer names; these are classed as confidential and were removed."
distractors: "The model was last retrained six months ago."
explanation: Persona tells the model which role to adopt; instructions state the task; output format states how the answer must be presented; data classification governs what data may be included, here confirmed by stating that confidential items were removed. The model's retraining date is not a prompt component.

question: A company classifies its data as Public, Internal or Confidential. Device configurations and customer records are Confidential; the IP addressing plan and site list are Internal. Policy states that only Public data may be sent to external generative AI services. Which prompt may an engineer send to an external AI chatbot?
options: "Here is our core switch running configuration, with the type 7 passwords left in because they are encrypted. Explain why OSPF is failing."
"Treat the following as confidential and do not store it. Here is our customer list with circuit IDs. Which circuits share a PE router?"
"Act as a network instructor. Explain, as a numbered list, how OSPF elects a designated router on a broadcast segment."
"Here is our IP addressing plan and site list. Suggest a summarisation scheme and return it as a table."
rationales: Wrong: Device configurations are Confidential under the policy, and type 7 is a weak, reversible encoding that does not protect the passwords.
Wrong: Customer records are Confidential. An instruction in the prompt does not control how the external service handles data or change its classification.
Correct: The prompt contains only general, publicly available knowledge and no company data, so it complies. It also gives a persona, an instruction and an output format.
Wrong: The addressing plan and site list are classified Internal, and only Public data may be sent to an external service.
explanation: Check the classification of everything in a prompt before sending it. Only data that policy allows may leave the organisation; asking the model to be discreet, or relying on weak type 7 obfuscation, does not change the classification.

question: An engineer wants a generative AI tool to turn a pasted list of 40 VLAN IDs and names into data that a Python script can load without any manual editing. Which prompt is most likely to produce output that can be used directly?
options: "Put the VLAN list below into a neat, easy-to-read format that I can paste into my script later."
"Act as a Python developer. Explain, step by step, how a script could read a list of VLAN IDs and names from a file."
"Summarise the VLAN list below in a short paragraph that is suitable for pasting into a change record."
"Convert the VLAN list below into a JSON array of objects with the keys vlan_id (integer) and name (string). Return only the JSON, with no commentary."
rationales: Wrong: "Neat" does not define a format. The model might return a table, bullet points or prose, none of which the script can be relied on to parse.
Wrong: This has a persona but asks for an explanation, so the answer would be advice about scripting, not the converted data.
Wrong: A prose summary is intended for people to read and cannot be loaded by a script as structured data.
